topics.title: Algebraic Expressions
learningObjectives: Apply the index laws to positive, negative, fractional and zero indices, and manipulate surds including rationalising denominators (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.1/2.2, AQA 7357 B1-B2, OCR A H640 2.01
Expand single and double brackets, recognising and deploying the difference of two squares and perfect square expansions (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.1, AQA 7357 B3
Factorise quadratics with a = 1 and a is not 1 using the AC method, and factorise expressions by grouping (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B3
Simplify, multiply, divide, add and subtract algebraic fractions by factorising and cancelling whole factors only (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B8

Divide polynomials by linear expressions using long division or the remainder theorem, and use the factor theorem to extract linear factors and unknown coefficients (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B4
Combine these skills fluently to prove simple statements and simplify harder expressions under timed exam conditions (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Collect like terms: only terms with identical variables and powers combine - 3x^2y and 3xy^2 are not like terms.
Index laws: x^a x x^b = x^(a+b), x^a / x^b = x^(a-b), (x^a)^b = x^(ab), x^0 = 1, x^(-a) = 1/x^a.
Difference of two squares a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); perfect squares a^2 +/- 2ab + b^2 = (a +/- b)^2.
In algebraic fractions, factorise numerator and denominator fully, then cancel common FACTORS only - never terms joined by + or -.
Factor theorem: f(a) = 0 means (x - a) is a factor; remainder theorem: remainder on division by (x - a) is f(a).
topics.exampleQuestion: Simplify fully (2x^2 + 3x - 2)/(x + 2) - (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2), and state the values of x for which the original expression is undefined. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Factorise both numerators: 2x^2 + 3x - 2 = (2x - 1)(x + 2) (M1: correct factorisation, AC method), and x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) (M1: difference of two squares). The first fraction becomes (2x - 1)(x + 2)/(x + 2) = 2x - 1 and the second becomes (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2) = x + 2 (M1: cancelling whole factors only). Subtracting: (2x - 1) - (x + 2) = x - 3 (A1: correct simplified form). The original expression is undefined at x = -2 and x = 2, where a denominator is zero - cancelling hides these restrictions, so state them (A1: restrictions identified).
practiceQuestions: Expand and simplify (3x - 2)(x + 4) - (x - 1)^2.
Factorise completely 6x^2 + 13x + 6, and hence simplify (6x^2 + 13x + 6)/(2x + 3).
Simplify (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4).
Divide 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 3x - 1 by (x - 2), giving the quotient and remainder, and verify the remainder using the remainder theorem.
Given f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6, show that (x - 1) is a factor and factorise f(x) completely.
Simplify (2x^2 y^(-3))^3 / (4x^(-1) y^2)^2, giving your answer with positive indices.

topics.title: Quadratic Equations
learningObjectives: Solve quadratic equations by factorising, including when the coefficient of x^2 is not 1 (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3
Complete the square for a = 1 and a is not 1, and use the completed square form to find exact roots and turning points (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3
Use the quadratic formula to solve any quadratic, leaving answers in exact surd form (AO1)
Interpret the discriminant to determine the number and nature of roots, including unknown-coefficient problems (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3
Use the relationships between roots and coefficients: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha beta = c/a (AO2)
Solve quadratic inequalities graphically and algebraically, giving answers in correct set notation (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.4, AQA 7357 B3
Solve hidden quadratic equations by substitution, back-substituting with the range of the substituted variable checked (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Standard form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a is not 0; factorising when a = 1 uses two numbers with product c and sum b; when a is not 1, use the AC method.
Completing the square: x^2 + bx = (x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2; for a is not 1, factor a out first.
Quadratic formula: x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/2a; always works, required for surd-form answers.
Discriminant b^2 - 4ac: > 0 two distinct real roots; = 0 one repeated root (tangency); < 0 no real roots. Sum of roots -b/a, product c/a.
Hidden quadratics: substitute u = x^2, u = sin(theta), u = e^x and solve in u, then back-substitute and CHECK the range of the substituted variable.
topics.exampleQuestion: Solve 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0, and hence solve 2sin^2(theta) - 5sin(theta) - 3 = 0 for 0 <= theta < 2pi. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Factorise: ac = -6, so 2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = 2x(x - 3) + 1(x - 3) = (2x + 1)(x - 3) = 0 (M1 A1), giving x = -1/2 or x = 3 (A1). Substituting u = sin(theta) (M1): sin(theta) = -1/2 or sin(theta) = 3. Since -1 <= sin(theta) <= 1, sin(theta) = 3 is impossible and is rejected (B1: range check). For sin(theta) = -1/2, the reference angle is pi/6, and sine is negative in quadrants 3 and 4 (M1), giving theta = pi + pi/6 = 7pi/6 and theta = 2pi - pi/6 = 11pi/6 (A1 A1).
practiceQuestions: Solve 3x^2 + 10x - 8 = 0 by factorising.
Solve x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0 by completing the square, giving exact surd answers.
Use the quadratic formula to solve 5x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0, leaving your answers in surd form.
Find the set of values of k for which kx^2 + 4x + k = 0 has real roots.
Solve the inequality x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0, giving your answer in set notation.
A rectangle has area 24 cm^2 and perimeter 20 cm. Find its dimensions.

topics.title: Coordinate Geometry
learningObjectives: Find the equation of a line from a gradient and point or from two points, in y = mx + c or ax + by + c = 0 form (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1, AQA 7357 C1
Calculate distances and midpoints, and use the parallel (m1 = m2) and perpendicular (m1 m2 = -1) conditions (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1, AQA 7357 C1
Find the equation of a circle from its centre and radius, and recover centre and radius by completing the square from the expanded form (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.6, AQA 7357 C2
Use circle properties: the radius is perpendicular to the tangent, and the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.6, AQA 7357 C2
Find intersections of lines with lines and lines with circles, interpreting a zero discriminant as tangency and deriving exact chord lengths (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1/3.6
Determine loci of points satisfying distance conditions and prove geometric facts using gradients and distances (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1); line through (x1, y1): y - y1 = m(x - x1).
Distance d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2); midpoint M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2).
Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines have gradients multiplying to -1 (m1 x m2 = -1).
Circle: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 with centre (a, b), radius r; radius is perpendicular to the tangent; the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.
Line-circle intersection: substitute and examine the resulting quadratic - discriminant zero means tangency; chord length follows from the two roots.
topics.exampleQuestion: Find the equation of the circle with diameter endpoints A(1, 2) and B(5, 6), and find the equation of the tangent at A. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Centre = midpoint of AB = ((1 + 5)/2, (2 + 6)/2) = (3, 4) (M1). AB = sqrt((5 - 1)^2 + (6 - 2)^2) = sqrt(32), so r^2 = 32/4 = 8 (M1 A1). Circle: (x - 3)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 8 (A1). Gradient of the radius from (3, 4) to A(1, 2) is (2 - 4)/(1 - 3) = 1 (M1), so the tangent gradient is -1 (perpendicular to radius). Tangent at A: y - 2 = -1(x - 1), i.e. y = -x + 3 (A1).
practiceQuestions: Find the equation of the line through (-2, 3) perpendicular to 2x + 3y = 6, in the form ax + by + c = 0.
Find the intersection of y = 2x - 1 and 3x + y = 7.
Find the tangent to the circle (x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25 at the point (5, 3).
Points A(1, 1), B(2, 2) and C(4, 0). Show that triangle ABC is right-angled, stating the right angle.
Show that the line 3x + 4y = 25 is a tangent to the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 and find the point of contact.
The line y = 2x + 1 intersects the circle (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 10 at A and B. Find the exact length AB.

topics.title: Trigonometry
learningObjectives: Work in radians and degrees, using s = r(theta) and A = 1/2 r^2 (theta) for arcs and sectors, and recall exact values for 0, pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2 (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.1-5.2, AQA 7357 E1
Sketch sin, cos and tan graphs and their transformations y = a sin(bx + c) + d, stating amplitude, period and phase (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.1, AQA 7357 E1
Use the core identities sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 and tan = sin/cos to solve equations and prove identities (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.4, AQA 7357 E4
Apply compound angle, double angle and R-formula results, including expressing a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) as R sin(theta + alpha) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.5, AQA 7357 E6
Solve trigonometric equations in a given interval, using the CAST diagram or graphs and rejecting impossible solutions (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.4, AQA 7357 E4
Apply the sine rule (including the ambiguous case), cosine rule and area = 1/2 ab sin C to triangles (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.3, AQA 7357 E3
Use inverse trigonometric functions with their domains and ranges, and small-angle approximations (AO1/AO2)
keyPoints: Exact values: sin: 0, 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, 1; cos: 1, sqrt(3)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1/2, 0 for pi/6 steps from 0 to pi/2; tan = sin/cos.
Core identity: sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1; tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta) when cos(theta) is not 0.
Compound angles: sin(A +/- B) = sin A cos B +/- cos A sin B; cos(A +/- B) = cos A cos B -/+ sin A sin B; double angle: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A in three forms.
R-formula: a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) = R sin(theta + alpha), R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), tan(alpha) = b/a; maximum R, minimum -R.
Sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C (ambiguous case SSA); cosine rule a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A; area = 1/2 ab sin C.
topics.exampleQuestion: Solve 2sin(2theta) = sqrt(3)cos(theta) for 0 <= theta < 2pi. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 6 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Expand sin(2theta) = 2sin(theta)cos(theta): 2(2sin(theta)cos(theta)) = sqrt(3)cos(theta) (M1: double angle). Rearrange and factorise: 4sin(theta)cos(theta) - sqrt(3)cos(theta) = 0, so cos(theta)(4sin(theta) - sqrt(3)) = 0 (M1: factorise rather than divide, preserving all solutions). Case 1: cos(theta) = 0 gives theta = pi/2 and theta = 3pi/2 (A1). Case 2: sin(theta) = sqrt(3)/4 = 0.4330 (M1: reference angle), giving theta = arcsin(0.4330) = 0.448 and theta = pi - 0.448 = 2.694 (A1 A1). All four solutions lie in the interval.
practiceQuestions: Prove that tan(2theta) = 2tan(theta)/(1 - tan^2(theta)).
Solve 3cos(2theta) + sin(theta) = 1 for 0 <= theta < 360 degrees.
Express 3sin(theta) + 4cos(theta) in the form R sin(theta + alpha), R > 0, and state the minimum value.
In triangle ABC, a = 7, b = 9 and angle C = 60 degrees. Find c and the area of the triangle.
Sketch y = 2cos(2x - pi/3) for 0 <= x <= 2pi, stating the amplitude, period and the x-coordinate of the first maximum.
Find the exact value of sin(arcsin(3/5) + arccos(4/5)).

topics.title: Differentiation
learningObjectives: Differentiate x^n from first principles for positive integer n and understand the first principles definition of the derivative (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.1, AQA 7357 G1
Apply the power rule to polynomials and to negative and fractional powers (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.2, AQA 7357 G2
Apply the sum, product, quotient and chain rules, including to e^x, ln x, sin x, cos x and tan x (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.5, AQA 7357 G2
Find equations of tangents and normals, using the perpendicular condition for the normal (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.3, AQA 7357 G3
Find and classify stationary points using the second derivative, including points of inflection (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.4, AQA 7357 G3
Solve optimisation problems, justifying maxima and minima, and use implicit differentiation and connected rates of change (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.6-7.7, AQA 7357 G3-G4
keyPoints: Power rule: d/dx(x^n) = n x^(n-1) for all real n; sum and difference differentiate term by term.
Product rule: d/dx(fg) = f'g + fg'; quotient rule: d/dx(f/g) = (f'g - fg')/g^2; chain rule: d/dx(f(g(x))) = f'(g(x)) x g'(x).
Standard derivatives: e^x, ln x = 1/x, sin x = cos x, cos x = -sin x, tan x = sec^2 x.
Stationary points: f'(x) = 0. Second derivative test: f'' < 0 maximum, f'' > 0 minimum; inflection requires f'' = 0 with sign change of f'.
Tangent gradient f'(x1); normal gradient -1/f'(x1). Implicit: differentiate term by term, y-terms get dy/dx factors. Connected rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt).
topics.exampleQuestion: Find the stationary points of y = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 and determine the nature of each. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: dy/dx = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1) (M1: differentiation, M1: factorisation). Stationary points where dy/dx = 0: x = 3 and x = -1 (A1). Second derivative: d^2y/dx^2 = 6x - 6 (M1). At x = 3: d^2y/dx^2 = 12 > 0, so a minimum (A1). At x = -1: d^2y/dx^2 = -12 < 0, so a maximum (A1). Coordinates: y(3) = -22 and y(-1) = 10, so minimum at (3, -22) and maximum at (-1, 10) (B1: coordinates stated).
practiceQuestions: Differentiate x sqrt(x + 2) using the product rule, simplifying your answer.
Find the equation of the normal to y = x^2 - 4x + 3 at the point where x = 2.
The radius of a sphere increases at 0.5 cm/s. Find the rate of increase of the volume when r = 10 cm.
For the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25, find dy/dx when x = 3 (y > 0).
Differentiate y = e^(3x) sin(2x), simplifying your answer.
Differentiate f(x) = 1/x from first principles.

topics.title: Integration
learningObjectives: Integrate polynomials and negative powers with the power rule, and recall the standard results for 1/x, e^x and basic trigonometric functions (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.1, AQA 7357 H1
Integrate composite functions using the reverse chain rule and substitution, changing limits correctly in definite integrals (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.2/8.5, AQA 7357 H2
Apply integration by parts, choosing u sensibly and repeating where needed (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.5, AQA 7357 H3
Evaluate definite integrals and find areas under and between curves, splitting where the curve crosses the axis (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.3, AQA 7357 H4
Calculate volumes of revolution about the x-axis and y-axis (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.4, AQA 7357 H4
Form and solve differential equations by separation of variables, finding particular solutions from initial conditions (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.6, AQA 7357 H5
keyPoints: Power rule: the integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not -1; special: 1/x gives ln|x| + C, e^x gives e^x + C.
Trig: the integral of sin x dx = -cos x + C; cos x dx = sin x + C; sec^2 x dx = tan x + C - always check the sign on sine.
Reverse chain rule: the integral of f'(x)[f(x)]^n dx = [f(x)]^(n+1)/(n+1) + C; the integral of f'(x)e^(f(x)) dx = e^(f(x)) + C.
Substitution: u = f(x), dx = du/f'(x), and CHANGE the limits for definite integrals. By parts: the integral of u dv = uv - the integral of v du; choose u by LIATE.

Definite integral F(b) - F(a) measures signed area: split where f crosses the axis. Area between curves: the integral of (top - bottom) dx. Volumes: V = (pi) times the integral of y^2 dx (x-axis) or (pi) times the integral of x^2 dy (y-axis).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the integral from 0 to 2 of x sqrt(4 - x^2) dx using the substitution u = 4 - x^2. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: u = 4 - x^2, so du/dx = -2x and x dx = -du/2 (M1: substitution and differential). Change the limits: x = 0 gives u = 4, and x = 2 gives u = 0 (B1: limits changed). The integral becomes the integral from 4 to 0 of u^(1/2) (-1/2) du = (1/2) times the integral from 0 to 4 of u^(1/2) du (M1: rewritten, flipped). Evaluating: (1/2)[(2/3)u^(3/2)] from 0 to 4 = (1/3)(4^(3/2)) = (1/3)(8) = 8/3 (A1: exact answer).
practiceQuestions: Find the integral of (3x^2 - 2x + 5)e^(x^3 - x^2 + 5x) dx.
Use integration by parts to find the integral of x cos x dx.
Evaluate the integral from 0 to 1 of x/(1 + x^2)^2 dx.
Find the area of the region bounded by y = x^2 and y = 2x - x^2.
The curve y = sqrt(x) from x = 0 to x = 4 is rotated a full turn about the x-axis. Find the exact volume formed.
Use integration by parts twice to find the integral of x^2 e^x dx.

topics.title: Vectors
learningObjectives: Represent vectors in 2D and 3D using components and unit vectors, and calculate magnitudes and direction angles (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 Section J, OCR A H640 14.01
Add, subtract and scalar-multiply vectors, and use position vectors to find displacements, midpoints and collinear points (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J1-J2

Calculate the scalar (dot) product in component and magnitude form, and determine angles between vectors and conditions for perpendicularity and parallelism (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J2-J3
Find the vector and Cartesian equations of a line in 2D and 3D, and determine whether lines are parallel, intersecting or skew (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J3
Solve geometric problems using vectors, proving properties such as right angles, parallelograms and collinearity (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, OCR A H640 14.01
Connect vectors to kinematics (velocity and displacement as vector quantities) and understand scalar triple product contexts as a Further Mathematics extension (AO2)
keyPoints: Magnitude: |a| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) in 2D and sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) in 3D; unit vector in the direction of a: a/|a|.
Displacement from A to B: AB = b - a (subtract position vectors: end minus start).
Scalar product: a . b = |a||b|cos(theta) = x1x2 + y1y2 + z1z2; perpendicular exactly when a . b = 0; parallel when components are in the same ratio.
Vector equation of a line: r = a + t d (or r = a + t(b - a) through two points); Cartesian form (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n.
In 3D, intersecting lines: solve two equations for t and s, then CHECK the third equation - failure means the lines are skew.
topics.exampleQuestion: The points A and B have position vectors a = (2, 1, 3) and b = (5, 3, 7). Find the vector AB, the distance AB, and a unit vector in the direction of AB. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 6 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AB = b - a = (5 - 2, 3 - 1, 7 - 3) = (3, 2, 4) (M1: subtract position vectors, A1). Distance: |AB| = sqrt(3^2 + 2^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 4 + 16) = sqrt(29) (M1 A1). Unit vector: AB/|AB| = (1/sqrt(29))(3, 2, 4), i.e. (3/sqrt(29), 2/sqrt(29), 4/sqrt(29)) (A1 A1: direction preserved, magnitude 1).
practiceQuestions: Find the angle between a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (2, 1, 0), in degrees to 1 d.p.
Find the value of x for which a = (2, -1, 3) and b = (1, x, -2) are perpendicular.
Find the vector equation of the line through A(1, 2, 0) with direction (2, -1, 4), and its Cartesian form.
Show that the points P(1, 2), Q(3, 4) and R(5, 6) are collinear.
Lines L1: r = (1, 2, 2) + t(1, 1, 0) and L2: r = (1, 5, 1) + s(2, -1, 1). Determine whether they intersect, and if so find the point.
A(1, 1), B(4, 2) and C(6, 5) are three vertices of parallelogram ABCD. Find the position vector of D.

topics.title: Algebraic Methods and Proof
learningObjectives: Understand and use the structure of mathematical proof, proceeding from given assumptions through a chain of valid logical steps to the conclusion (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 1, AQA 7357 A1, OCR A H640 1.01
Prove statements by deduction and by exhaustion, and prove algebraic identities using the equivalence sign (AO2) - AQA 7357 A1, Edexcel 9MA0 1.1-1.2
Disprove a statement by counter-example, selecting one value satisfying the conditions for which the claim fails (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 1.3, AQA 7357 A1

Carry out proofs by contradiction, including the irrationality of sqrt(2) and the infinitude of the primes (AO2) - AQA 7357 A1, OCR A H640 1.01; Edexcel tests contradiction-style arguments in past papers
Decompose proper rational functions into partial fractions with distinct and repeated linear factors, dividing improper fractions first (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B8
Select and justify the correct proof technique and write arguments in full sentences showing every logical step (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Deduction chains known facts into the conclusion; exhaustion proves every case in a finite split; a single counter-example disproves a general claim.
Contradiction: assume the statement false, derive an impossible consequence, conclude the original statement is true.
Identities use the equivalence sign and hold for all values of the variable; manipulate each side independently.
Partial fraction forms: A/(ax+b) + B/(cx+d) for distinct linear factors; A/(ax+b) + B/(ax+b)^2 for a repeated factor; divide improper fractions first.
Proofs are marked on structure: state the assumption or case split, show every logical step, state the contradiction or conclusion explicitly.
topics.exampleQuestion: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many prime numbers. (AQA 7357-style, 5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Assume, for contradiction, that there are finitely many primes, listed p_1, p_2, ..., p_n (M1: assumption stated). Let N = p_1 p_2 ... p_n + 1 (M1: construction). When N is divided by any listed prime p_i, the remainder is 1, so no p_i divides N (A1: valid deduction). Therefore N is either prime itself or has a prime factor that is not in the list - in both cases a prime exists outside the assumed complete list (A1: contradiction identified). This contradicts the assumption that the list contained all primes, so there must be infinitely many primes (A1: conclusion stated in words).
practiceQuestions: Prove by contradiction that sqrt(2) is irrational.
Disprove by counter-example the statement: for all real x, x^2 > x.
Prove that n^3 - n is divisible by 3 for all positive integers n.
Express (3x^2 + 7x - 2)/((x - 1)(x + 2)^2) in partial fractions.
Express (2x^2 + 3x + 5)/(x + 1)^2 in partial fractions.
Prove by exhaustion that every perfect square ends in the digit 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.

topics.title: Probability and Distributions
learningObjectives: Use Venn diagrams, tree diagrams and the addition and multiplication laws, including conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 13, AQA 7357 M1-M3
Determine whether two events are independent (P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)) or mutually exclusive, and use these conditions in problems (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 13, AQA 7357 M3
Model a situation with the binomial distribution B(n, p), checking the four conditions, and calculate probabilities and E(X) = np, Var(X) = np(1 - p) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 14, AQA 7357 N1-N2
Model with the normal distribution N(mu, sigma^2), standardising with Z = (X - mu)/sigma, and solve forward and inverse problems (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 14, AQA 7357 N3
Conduct hypothesis tests on a binomial model: state H0 and H1, find the critical region or p-value, and conclude in context (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 15, AQA 7357 O1-O2
Select an appropriate distribution for a context and justify the choice; understand the central limit theorem idea for large samples (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 14, AQA 7357 N1
keyPoints: Addition law: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); mutually exclusive events simplify it to P(A) + P(B).
Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B); independence: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A).
Binomial X ~ B(n, p): P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n-r); E(X) = np, Var(X) = np(1 - p); conditions: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independent trials.
Normal X ~ N(mu, sigma^2): standardise Z = (X - mu)/sigma; the 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68.3% within 1 sigma, 95.4% within 2 sigma, 99.7% within 3 sigma.
Hypothesis test: H0 (no change) against H1 (one- or two-tailed); reject H0 when the test statistic falls in the critical region or the p-value is below the significance level; conclude in context.
topics.exampleQuestion: A coin is tossed 20 times and 15 heads are observed. Test, at the 5% level of significance, whether the coin is biased. State your hypotheses clearly and conclude in context. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Let p be the probability of heads. H0: p = 0.5 (the coin is fair); H1: p is not 0.5 (the coin is biased) (B1 M1: hypotheses with the parameter). Two-tailed test, so the significance is 2.5% in each tail (B1: tail split stated). Under H0, X ~ B(20, 0.5), where X is the number of heads (B1: model stated). P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 0.0207 (M1 A1: p-value from tables or calculator). Since 0.0207 < 0.025, the result falls in the critical region, so reject H0 (A1: comparison and decision). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased towards heads (A1: conclusion in context).
practiceQuestions: State the four conditions required for a binomial model, and give a situation where one fails.

keyPoints: Edexcel LDS: weather data from 8 stations - 5 UK (Heathrow, Hurn, Leeming, Leuchars, Camborne) and 3 overseas (Beijing, Jacksonville, Perth) - for 1987 (May to October) and 2015 (full year).
Edexcel variables: daily mean temperature, total rainfall, total sunshine, mean windspeed and direction (Beaufort), mean cloud cover (oktas), mean pressure (hPa), mean gust.

Data cleaning: tr means trace rainfall (below 0.05 mm); n/a means not available; outliers flagged by the 1.5 x IQR rule.
Sampling: census (all), simple random (random numbers), systematic (every kth after a random start), stratified (proportional), quota and opportunity (non-random, prone to bias).
topics.exampleQuestion: The Edexcel large data set contains daily mean temperature data for Heathrow in 1987 and 2015. A student compares the mean of all the 1987 data with the mean of all the 2015 data and concludes that the climate at Heathrow cooled between the two years. Give two reasons why this comparison may be misleading, and suggest how a fairer comparison could be made. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 4 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: The 1987 data covers only May to October, while the 2015 data covers the full calendar year, so the two means are not based on the same months - the seasonal structure differs (B1: unlike-for-like comparison identified). A single year is weather rather than climate, so one year's mean against another's does not establish a trend (B1: interpretation). A fairer comparison restricts both years to the same months - for example comparing May to October 1987 with May to October 2015 - or takes samples of the same size in the same way from both years (B1 B1: fairer comparison described).

keyPoints: SUVAT (constant acceleration only): v = u + at, s = ut + 1/2 at^2, s = 1/2 (u + v)t, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, s = vt - 1/2 at^2 - pick the equation missing the quantity you do not need.
Calculus kinematics: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt; backwards: s = integral of v dt, v = integral of a dt, with initial conditions fixing constants. Distance = integral of |v| dt.
Newton's second law: resultant force F = ma; weight = mg; resolve perpendicular and parallel to slopes (R = mg cos(theta), weight component mg sin(theta)).
Friction: at most F = mu R, opposing motion; reaches the maximum in limiting equilibrium. Connected particles: F = ma for each mass, solve simultaneously.
Projectiles: horizontal velocity u cos(theta) constant; vertical u sin(theta) with acceleration -g; at maximum height vertical velocity is 0.
topics.exampleQuestion: A mass of 4 kg slides down a slope inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the mass and the slope is 0.2. Find the acceleration of the mass down the slope. (g = 9.8 m/s^2) (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Resolve perpendicular to the slope: R = mg cos(30 degrees) = 4(9.8)(sqrt(3)/2) = 33.9 N (M1 A1: normal reaction). Friction opposes the motion (up the slope) with maximum value F = mu R = 0.2 x 33.9 = 6.79 N (M1 A1: friction model). Weight component down the slope: mg sin(30 degrees) = 4(9.8)(0.5) = 19.6 N (B1). Applying Newton's second law along the slope: 19.6 - 6.79 = 4a, so the resultant is 12.8 N (M1). a = 12.8/4 = 3.20 m/s^2 down the slope (A1).

Textual Variations and Representations
learningObjectives: Apply systematic methods from all language levels (lexis/semantics, grammar, pragmatics, discourse, phonology/prosodics, graphology) to unseen spoken, written and electronic texts (AO1).
Analyse how mode, register, genre, audience and purpose shape meanings in a text, evidencing each with a linguistic choice (AO1/AO3).
Construct precise representation claims - 'the text represents X as...' - and advance them through every paragraph (AO1/AO3).
Select relevant contextual factors (mode, era, audience, production) rather than listing context indiscriminately (AO3).
Compare two texts through integrated points of similarity and difference instead of parallel text-by-text analysis (AQA Q3 / OCR H470/01 Section C).
Meet top-band descriptors (AQA Level 5; OCR 'confident' band) within exam timing: roughly 25 minutes per AQA text question and 20 for the comparison.
keyPoints: AQA Paper 1 Section A = 70 marks: Q1 Text A 25, Q2 Text B 25, Q3 comparison 20; Section B (children's language development) = 30 marks.
OCR H470/01 = 80 marks: Language under the microscope (2 x 10), Writing about a topical language issue (24), Comparing and contrasting texts (36).
Register = field + tenor + mode (Halliday & Hasan 1976): evidence each element with a linguistic choice.
A representation statement is a thesis: every paragraph must advance it - description without representation caps the mark.
Comparison must be integrated: point of comparison, then Text A evidence, then Text B evidence, then an explicit link.
AQA pairs texts from different modes and eras (June 2023: BBC News online, 2019 + The Bystander, 1928) - mode and context are the fastest AO3 route.
topics.exampleQuestion: Analyse how Text A uses language to create meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2023, Question 01 - Text A: a BBC News online article, March 2019)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO3, Level 5 requirements):

AO1 - conceptualised, systematic analysis: an opening thesis naming what Text A represents and through which genre/audience/purpose; then 4-6 paragraphs organised by representational angle, each applying methods from at least two language levels - lexis/semantics (e.g. connotative or emotive lexis building a semantic field), grammar (agency, transitivity, modality, nominalisation showing who acts and who is acted upon), pragmatics (presupposition, synthetic personalisation addressing the reader as 'you'), discourse (headline/standfirst structure, foregrounding, anecdote placement) and graphology (image, typography, hyperlink placement for the scrolling online reader). Every claim must be anchored in a precise quotation with accurate terminology and fluent written expression.

AO3 - relevant, woven context: the electronic mode of a 2019 online news article (immediacy, scannable short paragraphs, hyperlinks, searchable permanence, primary plus secondary search-driven audiences); news genre conventions (inverted pyramid, attributed sources); audience and purpose shaping choice. Context must be used to explain language, not listed.

What the top band adds: perceptive interpretation of the representation (what the text makes salient and why), consistent close analysis rather than feature-spotting, and a conclusion that returns to the representation thesis. The same logic applies to Question 02 on Text B.

For Question 03 (20 marks, comparison): integrated paragraphs organised by points of similarity and difference - e.g. shared covert purpose despite different modes; bolder, shorter syntax in the online text; historical lexis and longer syntax in the 1928 magazine - with differences explicitly attributed to mode, era and audience, and comparative connectives throughout.
practiceQuestions: Giving careful consideration to the context of the text, identify and analyse patterns of lexical and semantic use in Text A. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01, Section A, Question 1(a) - June 2023 wording)
Analyse how Text B uses language to create meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2023, Question 02 - Text B: a magazine article from The Bystander, April 1928)

Explore the similarities and differences in the ways these two texts use language: Text A is a company's email newsletter to customers; Text B is a transcript of the same company's customer-service live chat. [20 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Question 03 style)

learningObjectives: Classify word classes (open vs closed), phrase, clause and sentence types, and mood, and justify why each choice matters in an unseen text (AO1).
Apply semantic concepts - connotation, semantic fields, figurative language - to build representation claims rather than label devices (AO1/AO2).
