Push every point through the chain quotation - terminology - effect - context, selecting features rather than listing them (AO1/AO3).

Evaluate frameworks critically: name the theorist, apply the concept, then judge its explanatory power for the text (AO2 - AQA 'critical understanding'; OCR 'critical understanding of concepts and issues').
keyPoints: AQA 7702 examines frameworks through Paper 1 Section A (70 marks: Q1 25, Q2 25, Q3 20) and Paper 2 Q3 (40 marks, two-text discourses analysis); OCR's most direct framework test is H470/01 Section A 'Language under the microscope' (2 x 10 marks).
AO1 (both boards) = apply appropriate methods with associated terminology and coherent expression: feature-spotting without effect caps the mark.
AO2 = critical understanding of concepts and issues: name the framework (Grice, Austin/Searle, Brown & Levinson, Halliday, Kress & van Leeuwen), apply it, then evaluate its explanatory power.

AO3 = analyse and evaluate how contextual factors and language features construct meaning: mode determines which levels matter - prosodics for speech, graphology for print and electronic, multimodality for screen texts.
Selection beats coverage: four features pushed deep through quotation, terminology, effect and context outscore twelve named and dropped.
topics.exampleQuestion: Analyse how language in Text A creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Question 1 or 2 style; OCR equivalent: H470/01 Section C, 36 marks). Shorter-form version: using appropriate linguistic terminology, analyse the lexis, grammar and graphology of this short charity appeal. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01 Section A, 'Language under the microscope' style)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO2 + AO3, per the AQA 7702/1 levels-based mark scheme; OCR rewards the same through 'appropriate linguistic concepts and methods'):

Opening: a thesis - what the text represents (e.g. the crisis as urgent but solvable; the donor as the hero) and through which genre, audience and purpose (charity appeal; sympathetic mass audience; to persuade and collect).

AO1 - systematic methods (the analysis engine): (1) Lexis/semantics: a semantic field of need ('struggling', 'crisis') set against a field of hope ('change', 'future'); connotation carrying the representation; euphemism or dysphemism framing the cause. (2) Grammar: second-person pronouns and synthetic personalisation (Fairclough, 1989); imperative calls to action ('Donate now'); modal auxiliaries ('can', 'will') building epistemic confidence; transitivity casting the donor in material processes and the beneficiary in relational ones. (3) Pragmatics: presupposition that donation is expected ('your gift will...'); flouted quantity via statistics performing authority; indirect speech acts softening the ask. (4) Graphology/multimodality: bold totals, captioned images, white space and salience directing the eye to the ask (Kress & van Leeuwen's information value and salience).

AO2 - critical understanding: frameworks named and evaluated - e.g. Grice's maxims assumed then commercially exploited; Brown & Levinson's positive politeness ('you, together with us') building solidarity before the FTA of the request.

AO3 - context woven: the promotional mode, the mass/non-specialist audience constraining jargon, and the purpose (influence, not just inform) driving every choice - woven through, never listed.

Top band: perceptive, conceptualised analysis where every claim runs quotation → terminology → effect → context, and the representation thesis is advanced in every paragraph.
practiceQuestions: Using appropriate linguistic terminology, analyse the lexis and semantics of this short advertising copy. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01 Section A, 'Language under the microscope' style)
Analyse how language in this transcript of a doctor-patient consultation creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 style - spoken text)
Explore the similarities and differences in the ways that Text A and Text B use language to represent the same event. [20 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Q3 style)
Evaluate the idea that some language levels are more useful than others when analysing written texts. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A evaluation style)

Using appropriate linguistic concepts, analyse how graphological and multimodal features construct meanings in this social media post. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01 Section A, 'Language under the microscope' style)

topics.title: Language and Gender
learningObjectives: Outline and evaluate the deficit model (Jespersen; Lakoff 1975) with its criticisms of evidence and scope (AO2).
Evaluate dominance research - Zimmerman & West (1975), Fishman (1983) - including the interruption/overlap distinction and O'Barr & Atkins' (1980) 'powerless language' critique (AO2).
Assess the difference model (Tannen 1990) against diversity and dynamic approaches - Cameron (2007), Butler's (1990) performativity, Eckert & McConnell-Ginet's communities of practice (AO2).
Analyse how unseen media texts represent women and men through marked lexis, semantic derogation, agency and multimodal choices (AO1/AO3).
Deploy two or three theorists woven into an argument rather than listed, matching the AQA AO2 'evaluate the idea' essay demands (AO1/AO2).
Explain how contextual factors - era, domain (public/private), publication - shape gendered language use (AO3).
keyPoints: Lakoff (1975) 'women's language': hedges, tag questions, empty adjectives, intensifiers, superpolite forms, hypercorrect grammar, rising intonation on declaratives.
O'Barr & Atkins (1980): courtroom 'powerless language' correlates with social status, not sex - the standard AO2 critique of the deficit model.
Zimmerman & West (1975): men made almost all recorded interruptions in cross-sex conversations; Fishman (1983): women do the 'housework' of talk - topic-raising, questions, minimal responses.
Tannen (1990): report talk vs rapport talk; difference is cultural mismatch, not domination.
Cameron (2007): differences are small, within-gender variation exceeds between-gender; the difference model is a 'zombie' statistic recycled by publishers.
Butler (1990): gender is performed through repeated stylistic acts; Eckert & McConnell-Ginet: styles emerge in communities of practice.

AQA 7702/2 Section A = one 'Evaluate the idea that...' essay, 30 marks; OCR H470/02 Section B (Language in the media) = investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings, 24 marks.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the idea that a person's language use is completely determined by the social groups they belong to. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2017, Question 01)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO2 + AO3, 30 marks):

AO1: fluent, coherent essay with accurate terminology (hedges, tag questions, interruptions, report/rapport talk, communities of practice) and a clear argumentative line sustained from thesis to verdict.

AO2 - evaluating the idea (the core of the essay): the idea must be tested, not merely illustrated.
(1) Evidence for group influence: Lakoff's (1975) 'women's language' features as socialisation into tentativeness; Zimmerman & West's (1975) cross-sex interruption findings and Fishman's (1983) conversational 'housework' showing gendered patterns of talk; occupational and regional varieties conditioning registers.
(2) Evidence against complete determination: O'Barr & Atkins (1980) - 'powerless language' tracks status, not sex, so groups do not fix style; Cameron (2007) - within-gender variation exceeds between-gender; Hyde (2005) - gender similarities on most variables; Butler (1990) and Eckert & McConnell-Ginet - gender is performed and built in communities of practice, so speakers exceed their categories.
(3) Refined verdict: social groups shape access to registers and constrain style (deficit/dominance data are real), but 'completely determined' fails against within-group variation and contextual style-shifting - language use is conditioned, not determined.

AO3: contexts decide the case - public vs private domains (broadcast phone-ins vs Fishman's domestic data), era of research (1970s samples predate contemporary audiences), medium (interruption in face-to-face talk vs online chat), and the ideological context in which the deficit model was produced. Context woven through the evaluation, not appended.

Top-band marker: an explicit, defended verdict plus theorists used as evidence and critique (two or three, integrated), with awareness that the models themselves carry ideological baggage.
practiceQuestions: Evaluate the idea that women's language is deficient. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)

Using your understanding of relevant ideas and concepts, investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings in this magazine article about women in the workplace. [24 marks] (OCR H470/02, Section B - Language in the media, June 2023 wording)
Evaluate Tannen's difference model of language and gender. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)
Evaluate the claim that interruptions signal male dominance in conversation. [25 marks] (AQA-style AO2/AO3 essay)
Explain how semantic derogation supports the male-as-norm view of language. Illustrate with examples. [10 marks] (OCR ExamBuilder-style AO2/AO1 question)

topics.title: Language and Power and Technology
learningObjectives: Distinguish power in discourse from power behind discourse (Fairclough 1989) and instrumental from influential power, with textual evidence for each (AO1/AO2).
Apply Goffman's (1967) face and Brown & Levinson's (1987) politeness theory - positive/negative face, FTAs, mitigation strategies - to transcripts and media texts (AO1/AO3).
Analyse occupational power using Wareing (1999): vertical vs horizontal power, jargon as gatekeeping, and workplace discourse features (AO1/AO2).
Use the CDA three-dimensional method (description, interpretation, explanation) to link textual features to ideology and institutional power (AO1/AO3).
Analyse electronic language: multimodality (Kress & van Leeuwen 2006), CMC features (synchronicity, permanence, interactivity) and power online (AO1/AO3).
Deploy politeness and power concepts in directed writing for electronic and specialist audiences (AQA 7702/2 Q4; OCR H470/01 Section B) (AO1/AO2).
keyPoints: Fairclough (1989): power in discourse (visible in the encounter) vs power behind discourse (institutions setting conventions); instrumental vs influential power.
CDA method: description (text) - interpretation (discursive practice) - explanation (social practice/ideology).
Brown & Levinson (1987): positive face (approval) vs negative face (autonomy); FTAs mitigated by bald on-record, positive politeness, negative politeness, off-record, or avoidance.
Goffman (1967): face = the positive social value claimed in interaction; face-work maintains it.
Wareing (1999): vertical (hierarchical) vs horizontal (peer) occupational power; jargon gatekeeps; Koester (2004): phatic talk builds workplace solidarity.
Sinclair & Coulthard (1975): IRF/IRE - the teacher controls classroom turns and topics.
Crystal (2001): e-language as a third mode blending speech and writing; synchronous vs asynchronous CMC.
Electronic power: gatekeeping lowered (anyone can publish) but re-concentrated in platforms, algorithms and moderation; synthetic personalisation scales online.
AQA 7702/2 Section A = one 'Evaluate the idea...' essay (30); Q3 analyse discourses (40); Q4 directed writing (30). OCR H470/02 Section B Language in the media (24).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the idea that it is an advantage to be able to switch between different varieties of language. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 01)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO2 + AO3, 30 marks):

AO1: fluent, coherent argument with accurate terminology (code-switching, register, instrumental/influential power, positive/negative face, jargon, CMC affordances) sustained from thesis to verdict.

AO2 - evaluating the idea: test the claim, don't illustrate it.
(1) Evidence for the advantage: switching between registers gives access to instrumental and influential power - standard English and jargon unlock institutional gatekeeping (Wareing 1999); switching politeness strategies manages face across power distances (Brown & Levinson 1987); e-language demands a further switch (synchronous chat vs asynchronous email vs formal writing). O'Barr & Atkins (1980): high-status speakers command the powerful varieties - repertoire is a resource.
(2) Complexities and counters: switching is not equally available to all - repertoire reflects education and class, so the 'advantage' is unevenly distributed (a critical-linguistics point: Fairclough 1989 - unequal access to discourse power); value judgements attach to varieties, so switching can be read as 'selling out' or as insufficiently 'authentic'; Butler's (1990) performativity reframes switching as identity work, not mere advantage.
(3) Refined verdict: switching is an advantage where power is at stake - occupational, institutional, media - but it is a resource whose distribution is socially patterned, not a free good.

AO3: contexts decide - occupational settings (jargon gatekeeping), media and electronic settings (register shifts for platform audiences), public vs private domains, and the ideological context in which some varieties are ranked as standard.

Top-band marker: an explicit, defended verdict plus theorists used as evidence and critique, with awareness that the 'advantage' framing itself carries ideological weight.
practiceQuestions: Evaluate the idea that a person's language use is completely determined by the social groups they belong to. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2017, Question 01 - occupation/power focus)
Analyse how language in this hospital consultation transcript creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section A style - unequal encounter)

Using your understanding of relevant ideas and concepts, investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings in this online news article about workplace surveillance. [24 marks] (OCR H470/02, Section B - Language in the media, June 2023 wording)
Evaluate the claim that politeness strategies always signal social power. [25 marks] (AQA-style AO2/AO3 essay)
Explain how electronic mode shapes politeness in computer-mediated communication. Illustrate with examples. [10 marks] (OCR ExamBuilder-style synthesis question)

topics.title: Child Language Acquisition
learningObjectives: Sequence the stages of spoken development - pre-verbal, holophrastic, two-word, telegraphic, post-telegraphic - and label the stage in unseen data from linguistic evidence, not from age alone (AO1).
Analyse phonological development (substitution, deletion, assimilation, cluster reduction) and link phonological processes to lexical and grammatical growth (AO1).
Categorise virtuous errors - overextension, underextension, overgeneralisation - and explain why they evidence rule formation rather than failed imitation (AO1/AO2).
Evaluate theories critically: Chomsky's LAD and its critiques, Skinner's behaviourism, Piaget's cognitive model, Vygotsky's ZPD, Bruner's LASS and Halliday's functions (AO2).
Analyse reading and writing development (emergent literacy, Kroll's phases, Britton's modes) and compare spoken and written trajectories (AO1/AO2).
Apply the data-analysis method for AQA 7702/1 Section B (30 marks, AO1 15 + AO2 15) and OCR H470/02 Section A (20 marks, AO1 10 + AO2 10) within exam timing.
keyPoints: AQA 7702/1 Section B = 30 marks: a discursive essay, choice of two questions, data may be spoken, written or multimodal (June 2024: a child transcript and children's writing).
The June 2024 mark scheme splits Section B as AO1 15 + AO2 15: half data analysis, half critical evaluation of theories and the given statement - theory description alone cannot pass.
OCR H470/02 Section A = 20 marks (AO1 10 + AO2 10): the language development stage of a child aged 0-7, analysing phonology, grammar and meaning, with the IPA provided in the paper.
Label stages from evidence - utterance length, grammatical completeness, phonological processes - never from the child's age; mixed-stage data is normal and expected.
Theories work best in evaluation pairs: nature (Chomsky) vs nurture (Skinner); cognition-first (Piaget) vs interaction-first (Vygotsky/Bruner); functions (Halliday) cut across all four.
Virtuous errors are the single strongest classroom argument: systematic, rule-governed errors absent from adult input cannot be products of imitation alone.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Adults play the most important role in children's language development.' Referring to Data Set 1 in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2024, Question 4 - Section B)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AQA 7702/1 Section B: 30 marks = AO1 15 + AO2 15, per the June 2024 mark scheme):

AO1 - analysis of the data (15): open by identifying the stage(s) evidenced in Data Set 1 from linguistic evidence - utterance length, grammatical completeness, phonological processes - not from age alone. Then analyse systematically: phonology (substitutions, deletions, cluster reduction read against the transcription key - what the child can and cannot produce), lexis/semantics (Nelson's categories, overextension/underextension, concrete nominals dominant), grammar (negatives and questions against Bellugi's stages, missing auxiliaries and articles, overgeneralisation such as 'goed'), pragmatics (turn-taking, Halliday's functions, caregiver recasts and expansions visible in the data). Every point anchored in a precise quotation from the data set.

AO2 - critical evaluation of the view (15): evaluate the statement, don't describe it. Support: child-directed speech and scaffolding - Vygotsky's ZPD and the more knowledgeable other, Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976), Bruner's LASS - with recasts and expansions shaping development in the data. Challenge: Chomsky's LAD and the poverty of stimulus (grammar acquired from imperfect input), virtuous errors absent from adult speech ('goed', Berko & Brown's 1960 'fis'), Brown & Hanlon's (1970) finding that caregivers correct truth value rather than grammatical form, and cross-cultural evidence that acquisition proceeds on schedule where CDS is minimal. Judgement: interaction clearly matters, but it cannot explain rule formation alone - a balanced conclusion weighing both sides.

Discursive craft: both sides engaged, theories evaluated against data patterns rather than bolted on, explicit conclusion. Question 5 (the writing-development option) works identically: analyse the children's writing samples against Kroll's phases and emergent-literacy features (AO1), then evaluate the purpose-driven-writing claim against genre, audience and instruction research (AO2).
practiceQuestions: Using the appropriate terminology to explain your findings, examine the language development stage of the child-participant as evidenced in the transcript. You should identify and analyse the phonology, grammar and meaning of his utterances. Use your knowledge of theories and concepts of child language acquisition to support your answer. [20 marks] (OCR H470/02, June 2024, Question 1)

'Writing with a sense of purpose is the most important skill to develop when learning to write.' Referring to Data Set 2 in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2024, Question 5)
'Children learn to talk through imitation.' Referring to data and relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section B style)

Examine the phonological development evidenced in the transcript, using appropriate terminology, and support your answer with theories and concepts of child language acquisition. [20 marks] (OCR H470/02 Section A style)

'Children's early language is used mainly to get things they want.' Referring to data in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section B style)

topics.title: Language Change
learningObjectives: Distinguish internal change (analogy and regularisation, phonological erosion) from external change (borrowing, contact, technology) and illustrate both with dated examples (AO1/AO2).
Apply the lexis processes of change - borrowing, coinage, compounding, blending, clipping, backformation, conversion - and recognise archaisms and their discourse uses (AO1).
Analyse semantic shift through broadening, narrowing, amelioration and pejoration, with ready-made example pairs (AO2).
Trace the standardisation chronology - Caxton 1476, Johnson 1755, Lowth 1762, Alford 1864, the 1870 Education Act, the BBC and OED - and evaluate Johnson's prescriptivism in aims and practice (AO2).
Evaluate the prescriptivism vs descriptivism debate - Aitchison's models, Cameron's verbal hygiene, the Beale/Partridge prescriptive tradition - and avoid nostalgia arguments (AO2).
Analyse change data: the OCR H470/02 Section C two-text comparison (36 marks) and the AQA 7702/2 evaluative essay (30 marks, AO1 10 + AO2 20).
keyPoints: AQA 7702/2 Section A = 30 marks: a choice of two evaluative essays - language diversity or language change - marked AO1 10 + AO2 20 (June 2023 mark scheme).

OCR H470/02 Section C = 36 marks: two texts from different periods (1600s to present), analysing variations and how contextual factors construct meaning; roughly 15 minutes preparation plus 50 minutes writing.
Johnson (1755) was prescriptive in ambition - to 'fix' and 'ascertain' the language - but descriptive in practice: his Dictionary records usage with literary citations and 'offers no law'.
Aitchison's three models (damp spoon, crumbling castle, infectious disease) are straw men to dismantle, not theories to accept - each fallacy has a named counter-argument.
Every change needs a cause (internal or external), a route (S-curve diffusion, lexical diffusion, waves) and an attitude (prescriptivist or descriptivist) - structure essays around that triad.
The semantic-shift quadrants - broadening/narrowing crossed with amelioration/pejoration - supply dateable examples: 'silly', 'pretty', 'meat', 'dog', 'villain'.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the idea that language change is caused by contact between different social groups. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 2 - Section A)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AQA 7702/2 Section A: 30 marks = AO1 10 + AO2 20, per the June 2023 mark scheme):

AO1 - language examples with accurate methods (10): the evaluation runs on precise, dated evidence: borrowing layers (Norse 'skirt'/'shirt' and 'they/them'; Norman French 'beef'/'cow' register split; colonial 'shampoo'; global 'sushi'); coinage and word formation from contact and technology ('selfie', 'brexit'); semantic shift where contact drives meaning (amelioration and pejoration following prestige contact); etymology and word-formation terminology applied accurately throughout.

AO2 - critical understanding of concepts and issues (20): the claim must be evaluated, not described. Support: contact is the best-documented route of external change - invasion, trade and migration demonstrably reshaped English lexis (the Norman Conquest is the textbook case); substratum and prestige explanations explain which loans survive; globalisation and digital contact accelerate 21st-century borrowing. Challenge: substantial change happens without contact - internal analogy and regularisation ('holp' to 'helped', kine to cows), phonological erosion of inflections, and the Great Vowel Shift whose causes are debated and internal; other explanations - functional theory (need), S-curve diffusion (internal mechanics of spread), random fluctuation (Hockett) - cover what contact cannot. Judgement: contact is a major cause, but a partial one: internal forces and standardisation also shape change, so the claim holds for lexis more than for grammar and phonology.

Essay craft: define 'contact' and 'change' first; evaluate both sides with named linguists (Aitchison, Crystal, Hockett, Chen) and dated examples; reach an explicit judgement. The same logic answers the diversity option (Question 1): evaluate the claim about varieties with code-switching research and standard-language ideology, then judge.
practiceQuestions: By detailed analysis of the writing in both passages, discuss and illustrate variations in language between the early years of the 20th and the 21st centuries. In your answer you should explore the ways language is used in each text as well as how contextual factors influence the way meaning is constructed. [36 marks] (OCR H470/02, June 2024, Question 3)
Evaluate the idea that the English language is in decline. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)
Evaluate the idea that new words entering the language weaken it. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)

By detailed analysis of the writing in both passages, discuss and illustrate variations in language between the 17th and 21st centuries. In your answer you should explore the ways language is used in each text as well as how contextual factors influence the way meaning is constructed. [36 marks] (OCR H470/02 Section C style)
Evaluate the idea that it is an advantage to be able to switch between different varieties of language. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 1 - Section A diversity option)

topics.title: Language Discourses
learningObjectives: Identify language discourses - texts debating language use, change, diversity, gender and power - and connect them to the wider debates they draw on (AO2).
Analyse attitudes and perspectives: how texts represent language, construct the producer's identity and position the reader (AQA spec 4.2.3; AO1/AO3).
Deploy the discursive-device catalogue - prescriptive claims, anecdotes, appeals to authority, modality, evaluative lexis, metaphor, hyperbole - as evidence of stance (AO1/AO3).
Compare how two texts present views on a language issue, evaluating how effectively each presents its case (AQA 7702/2 Question 3, 40 marks: AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15).
Write a directed or opinion piece for a non-specialist audience: assess ideas from the texts, refer to ideas from language study, argue a view (AQA 7702/2 Question 4, 30 marks: AO2 20 + AO5 10).
Adapt to OCR's discourse tasks: Language in the media (H470/02 Section B, 24 marks: AO2 12 + AO3 12) and the topical-issue directed writing (H470/01 Section B, 24 marks).
keyPoints: AQA 7702/2 Section B: Question 3 = 40 marks (AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15) analysing how two texts present views; Question 4 = 30 marks (AO2 20 + AO5 10) - an opinion article.
AQA spec 4.2.3: discourse texts represent language, construct an identity for the producer, position the reader and connect to wider discourses about language - four bullets, four jobs.
Devices double as stance evidence: high modality + evaluative lexis + hyperbole + anecdote = prescriptive; hedging + corpus citation + named linguists = descriptivist.
June 2023's texts were both on the full stop (The Conservative Woman and MailOnline, 2020) - same issue, opposing personas: the examiner tests how each presents, not what they claim.
OCR places discourses in H470/02 Section B (Language in the media, 24 marks - multimodal text, AO2 12 + AO3 12) and H470/01 Section B (topical statement directed writing, 24 marks, ~500 words).
Question 4's three bullets are a checklist: assess the ideas and issues raised in Text A and Text B, refer to ideas from language study, argue your own views - hit all three or lose marks.
topics.exampleQuestion: Analyse how language is used in Text A and Text B to present views about changing uses of language. In your answer you should: examine any similarities and differences you find between the two texts; explore how effectively the texts present their views. [40 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 3 - Text A: The Conservative Woman, 2020; Text B: MailOnline, 2020, both on the full stop)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AQA 7702/2 Section B Question 3: 40 marks = AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15, per the June 2023 mark scheme):

AO1 - systematic analysis (10): lexis/semantics (evaluative lexis and semantic fields constructing the representation of language - decay vs preservation), grammar (high modality, declaratives, rhetorical questions, hyperbole), pragmatics (presuppositions, synthetic personalisation, irony, direct reader address), discourse (anecdotal openings, appeals to authority, structure), graphology (headline, images, layout) - each claim anchored in precise quotation with accurate terminology.

AO3 - context woven (15): the producers and audiences (a niche conservative blog vs a mass-circulation tabloid), the online mode of 2020 (clickbait headlines, shorter paragraphs, comment-enabled engagement), and the subject context - the wider discourse each text connects to (decline narrative, generational complaint). Context explains the language; it is never listed.

AO4 - connections and evaluation (15): integrated comparison - same issue, opposing or complementary presentations: similarities (both represent language change as a story, both use anecdote and authority), differences (persona - the exasperated purist vs the knowing reporter; register - polemical blog voice vs tabloid breeziness; evidence type - anecdote vs quotation). Then how effectively: judge whether each text's evidence supports its claim, whether its persona engages or alienates its audience, and whether its rhetoric fits its mode - the second bullet is where the top band lives.

Craft: every attitude claim anchored to a quoted device; comparative connectives throughout; the effectiveness judgement explicit in the conclusion. For Question 4 (30 marks = AO2 20 + AO5 10): assess both texts' ideas, deploy original language-study examples (Aitchison, Crystal, standard language ideology), argue a thesis in an engaging, accurate non-specialist register.
practiceQuestions: Write an opinion article on views about the changing uses of language. In your article you should: assess the ideas and issues raised in Text A and Text B; refer to ideas from language study; argue your own views. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 4)
'Americanisms are taking over the English language.' Write a speech for an English class arguing for or against the statement. Aim for 500 words. [24 marks] (OCR H470/01, June 2024, Question 2)

Using your understanding of relevant ideas and concepts, investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings in this text. [24 marks] (OCR H470/02, June 2024, Question 2 - Language in the media: a multimodal media text)

Analyse how language is used in Text A and Text B to present views about the apostrophe. In your answer you should: examine any similarities and differences you find between the two texts; explore how effectively the texts present their views. [40 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section B Question 3 style)
Evaluate the idea that it is an advantage to be able to switch between different varieties of language. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 1 - Section A diversity option)

topics.title: Language Investigation and Original Writing (NEA)
learningObjectives: Choose and scope an investigation focus - gender, change, power, region, occupation or acquisition - framed as a precise question or hypothesis with named variables (AQA 7702/C; OCR H470/03).
Justify a methodology: data type (naturally occurring, elicited or corpus), sampling, transcription choices and the frameworks used for analysis (AO1/AO3).
Address ethics: informed consent, anonymisation, right to withdraw and secure storage, especially for data involving children (AO3).
Structure the investigation - introduction, methodology, analysis, conclusion - so findings are argued through language levels rather than described (AO1/AO3).
Target the AO profile of the AQA investigation (70 marks: AO1 20, AO2 20, AO3 20, AO4 10) and of the original writing task (750-word piece + 750-word commentary, 30 marks).
Meet the OCR H470/03 requirements: the research project plus the academic poster summarising title, data, method and findings.
Avoid the standard pitfalls: overbroad scope, data dumping, description without analysis and a commentary that narrates rather than reflects.
keyPoints: AQA 7702/C: language investigation max 2,000 words excluding data and quotes (70 marks: AO1 20, AO2 20, AO3 20, AO4 10) + one original writing piece (750 words) with a 750-word commentary (30 marks: AO4 15, AO5 15).
OCR H470/03: independent language research - a research project of about 2,500 words excluding data and appendices, plus an academic poster summarising it.
Focus areas: gender, change, power, region/dialect, occupation and acquisition - narrow each to a specific question ('How does X construct Y in Z?'), never a topic label.
Data: naturally occurring for authenticity, elicited for control, corpora (BNC/COCA) for scale - justify the choice and transcription method; address consent, anonymisation and withdrawal.
Analysis: argue findings through the relevant language levels (lexis, grammar, semantics, pragmatics, phonology/prosodics, graphology) with framework terminology, not impressionistic description.

Original writing: one piece for a real audience and purpose; the commentary must reflect on choices (lexis, syntax, tone, structure) against audience and purpose and connect to style models - reflection, not narration of process.
Pitfalls that cost marks: overbroad scope, data dumping, description without analysis, theory listed but never applied, no ethics section, commentary written as 'what I did'.
topics.exampleQuestion: Design a language investigation into an aspect of language and power: set out a precise title, the data and sampling method, ethical safeguards, the frameworks for analysis, and how each design choice targets the assessment objectives. (AQA 7702/C, 70 marks: AO1 20, AO2 20, AO3 20, AO4 10; the OCR H470/03 project sets the same demand, plus an academic poster.)
topics.modelAnswer: Model outline: 'How does doctor-patient talk distribute authority? A study of ten recorded GP consultations.' Title: a question with named variables and bounded data - instantly shows AO1 precision. Introduction: power in institutional talk (asymmetry of knowledge, goal orientation, gatekeeping) with two or three research sources woven in as tools, not a literature dump (AO2). Data and methodology: ten naturally occurring consultations recorded with written consent, orthographic transcription with pause and overlap notation, justification of the sample (same practice, comparable appointments) and its limits (AO3). Ethics: consent forms, pseudonymisation of doctors and patients, right to withdraw, secure storage and deletion - stated as applied mechanics (AO3). Analysis - three sections: (1) directives and imperatives: who issues them, who complies; (2) medical jargon as gatekeeping: asymmetry of specialist knowledge; (3) turn-taking and topic control: question chains, interruptions, agenda management. Each section argues findings through framework terminology with quantified evidence plus close discourse analysis of two contrasting extracts (AO1/AO3), links each finding to power concepts and institutional context (AO2/AO3) and connects patterns across the extracts (AO4). Conclusion: synthesise the three findings into a direct answer to the title question, note limitations (small sample, single practice) and suggest an extension (AO1/AO3). Full marks require accurate terminology throughout, critical rather than decorative use of research, context-sensitive analysis and explicit connections - description alone caps the mark in the middle bands.
practiceQuestions: Explain why a narrow focus produces stronger language investigations than a broad one. (AQA 7702/C, AO1/AO3)
Evaluate this investigation title: 'An investigation into language and gender.' What is wrong with it, and how would you reframe it?
Outline the ethical requirements for a language acquisition investigation using recordings of a child aged two to three.
What must the AQA original writing commentary do to hit AO4 and AO5? (30 marks: 15 + 15)
Identify three common pitfalls in NEA investigations and the marks each costs.

topics.title: Cell Structure
learningObjectives: Label and state the function of every eukaryotic organelle from light- and electron-microscope images (AQA 3.2.1.1; OCR 2.1.1)
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and describe viral structure (AQA 3.2.1.1; OCR 2.1.1)
Explain the fluid mosaic model and each transport mechanism, including water potential calculations (AQA 3.2.1.2/3.2.3; OCR 2.1.5)
Describe mitosis, calculate a mitotic index, and explain how meiosis generates variation (AQA 3.2.2, 3.4.3; OCR 2.1.6)
Link cell specialisation to function in erythrocytes, sperm and epithelia
Apply microscopy maths: magnification, resolution, graticule calibration and image-size calculations
keyPoints: Nucleus: DNA + nucleolus; mitochondrion: aerobic respiration with cristae; RER/SER: protein/lipid synthesis; Golgi: modify and package; lysosome: hydrolytic enzymes; chloroplast: photosynthesis; vacuole: turgor
Prokaryote: no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA + plasmids, peptidoglycan wall; eukaryote: 80S ribosomes, linear histone-bound DNA, membrane-bound organelles

Transport: simple diffusion (small, non-polar), facilitated diffusion (channel/carrier proteins), active transport (ATP, against gradient), osmosis (water, down water-potential gradient), co-transport, endo/exocytosis
Mitosis: prophase-metaphase-anaphase-telophase gives two identical diploid cells; meiosis: two divisions, crossing over and independent assortment give haploid gametes and variation
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.2.1.2, 6 marks): Describe the fluid mosaic model of the cell-surface membrane and explain how its structure results in selective permeability.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per linked point, 6 total): (1) Bilayer of phospholipids with hydrophilic phosphate heads outwards and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails inwards. (2) Membrane is fluid - phospholipids (and some proteins) can move laterally within the layer. (3) Proteins embedded in the bilayer form a mosaic - integral proteins span the membrane, peripheral proteins on the surface. (4) Hydrophobic core means small non-polar molecules cross freely by simple diffusion. (5) Polar molecules and ions cannot cross the core; they pass through channel/carrier proteins by facilitated diffusion (or are actively transported using ATP). (6) Cholesterol regulates fluidity/stability; glycoproteins and glycolipids act as receptors/antigens for recognition. Mark scheme awards structure-function links, not bare labels.
practiceQuestions: Describe the ultrastructural features of a prokaryotic cell that distinguish it from a eukaryotic cell. (4 marks)
Describe the sequence of events in mitosis (PMAT) and state the biological significance of the process. (6 marks)
Explain how the structure of the mitochondrion is adapted for efficient aerobic respiration. (4 marks)
A student views 400 cells in a root-tip squash; 36 show visible chromosomes. Calculate the mitotic index and explain why the value is low. (3 marks)
Explain the difference between simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport. (6 marks)
A plant cell and an animal cell are placed in pure water. Describe and explain what happens to each. (4 marks)

topics.title: Biological Molecules and Respiration
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides, triglycerides and phospholipids, and state the biochemical tests (AQA 3.1.1-3.1.3; OCR 2.1.2)
Explain protein structure levels and enzyme action via the induced fit model (AQA 3.1.4; OCR 2.1.4)
Interpret Km, Vmax and the effects of competitive and non-competitive inhibitors from rate graphs
Detail glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation with locations and yields (AQA 3.5.2; OCR 5.2.1)
Explain chemiosmosis and calculate theoretical vs actual ATP yield per glucose; calculate RQ values
Compare anaerobic respiration in animals (lactate) and yeast (ethanol) and explain the lower yield
keyPoints: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Link reaction (matrix): pyruvate → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH. Krebs (matrix): per acetyl CoA → 2CO₂ + 3NADH + FADH₂ + ATP
Oxidative phosphorylation: NADH/FADH₂ donate electrons to the ETC; proton pumping builds the gradient; H⁺ flows through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis); O₂ is the terminal electron acceptor
Theoretical yield ~32 ATP per glucose; actual 30-32 due to proton leak, shuttle costs and ATP spent transporting pyruvate/ADP
Anaerobic: animals pyruvate → lactate (lactate dehydrogenase, regenerates NAD⁺); yeast pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂
Enzymes: induced fit lowers activation energy; competitive inhibitors raise Km (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax
Tests: Benedict's (reducing sugar), Benedict's after HCl/NaHCO₃ (non-reducing), iodine (starch), Biuret (protein), emulsion (lipid)
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.5.2, 5 marks): Explain why respiration of one glucose molecule in anaerobic conditions produces far less ATP than in aerobic conditions.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 5 total): (1) Anaerobically glycolysis is the only stage operating - glucose is only partially oxidised to pyruvate, then to lactate (animals) or ethanol + CO₂ (yeast). (2) The link reaction, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation cannot run because NADH cannot be reoxidised via the electron transport chain. (3) Only the net 2 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis are produced. (4) Aerobically, oxidation of 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ pumps protons and drives chemiosmosis, yielding ~30 more ATP. (5) Without oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor the proton gradient cannot be maintained, so oxidative phosphorylation stops.
practiceQuestions: State where glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation occur, and give the net yield of glycolysis. (4 marks)
Explain how the structure of glycogen is related to its function as an energy store. (4 marks)
A non-competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme-catalysed reaction. Explain its effect on Vmax and contrast it with a competitive inhibitor. (5 marks)
Explain the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration. (3 marks)
Calculate the RQ for a substrate respired as: C₃H₆O₃ + 3 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 3 H₂O, and state what the value indicates. (3 marks)
Explain the induced fit model of enzyme action. (3 marks)

topics.title: Exchange and Transport
learningObjectives: Explain surface area to volume ratio and the features of efficient exchange surfaces (AQA 3.3.1; OCR 3.1.1)
Describe gas exchange in the alveoli, insects, fish and plants, and ventilation mechanics (AQA 3.3.2; OCR 3.1.1)
Describe digestion, absorption and co-transport of glucose in the ileum (AQA 3.3.3; Edexcel A T1/T2)
Describe the heart structure, cardiac cycle and blood vessels; explain tissue fluid formation (AQA 3.3.4; OCR 3.1.2)
Explain transpiration and the cohesion-tension theory; describe phloem translocation by mass flow (AQA 3.3.4.2; OCR 3.1.3)
Calculate cardiac output, ventilation rate and interpret potometer data
keyPoints: As size increases SA:V falls; efficient exchange surfaces: large area, thin, good gradient (Fick's law); mass transport systems overcome diffusion limits
Lungs: alveoli (large SA, thin squamous epithelium), capillary network, ventilation maintains gradient; insect tracheae: spiracles; fish: gill lamellae, counter-current; plants: stomata, mesophyll
Ileum absorption: microvilli, Na⁺-glucose co-transport (Na⁺/K⁺ pump → Na⁺ diffuses in dragging glucose → facilitated diffusion out)
Cardiac cycle: SAN → AVN → bundle of His → Purkyne fibres; systole/diastole; valves prevent backflow; cardiac output = HR × SV
Tissue fluid: hydrostatic pressure forces fluid out at arterial end; proteins stay in (oncotic pressure pulls water back); lymph drains excess
Xylem: cohesion-tension, transpiration pull, lignified walls; phloem: mass flow from source to sink; sucrose loaded actively at source
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.3.4.2, 5 marks): Explain how the cohesion-tension theory accounts for the movement of water from the roots to the leaves of a plant.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 5 total): (1) Water evaporates from mesophyll cells into air spaces and diffuses out through stomata (transpiration), lowering the water potential of the mesophyll cells. (2) Water therefore moves from the xylem into mesophyll cells by osmosis down the water-potential gradient. (3) This creates tension (transpiration pull) in the xylem column. (4) Cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) and adhesion to the lignified walls keep the water column unbroken and under tension. (5) The tension pulls water up as a continuous column from the roots, where water enters by osmosis (high root water potential), aided by root pressure.
practiceQuestions: Explain how the mammalian lung is adapted for efficient gas exchange. (5 marks)
Explain how counter-current exchange in fish gills maximises oxygen uptake. (4 marks)
Explain the co-transport of glucose in the ileum epithelium. (5 marks)
Describe the events of the cardiac cycle and explain how valves ensure unidirectional flow. (6 marks)
Calculate the cardiac output of a person with heart rate 70 bpm and stroke volume 70 cm³. (2 marks)
Explain how tissue fluid is formed and how excess tissue fluid is returned to the circulatory system. (5 marks)

topics.title: DNA, Genes and Protein Synthesis
learningObjectives: Describe DNA and RNA structure and explain why DNA is suited to carrying information (AQA 3.1.5.1; OCR 2.1.3.1)
Describe semi-conservative replication and the evidence from the Meselson-Stahl experiment (AQA 3.1.5.2; OCR 2.1.3.2)
Explain the features of the genetic code (triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate, universal) (AQA 3.4.1)
Describe transcription and post-transcriptional modification in eukaryotes (AQA 3.4.2; OCR 2.1.3.3)
Describe translation with codon-anticodon pairing and peptide bond formation (AQA 3.4.2; OCR 2.1.3.3)
Explain how gene mutations (substitution, insertion, deletion) alter protein structure (AQA 3.8.1; OCR 6.1.1)
keyPoints: DNA: antiparallel strands, A-T (2 H-bonds), G-C (3 H-bonds), sugar-phosphate backbone of phosphodiester bonds; RNA: ribose, uracil, single-stranded
Replication: helicase unwinds and unzips; DNA polymerase synthesises 5'→3' (leading continuous, lagging in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase)
Transcription: RNA polymerase, template strand, pre-mRNA spliced (introns out) in eukaryotes
Translation: ribosome reads codons; tRNA anticodons deliver amino acids; peptide bonds form the polypeptide
Mutations: substitution (silent/missense/nonsense), insertion/deletion (frameshift); mutagens increase rate
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.1.5.2, 5 marks): Describe semi-conservative replication of DNA and explain how the Meselson-Stahl experiment supports this model.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 5 total): (1) DNA helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing both antiparallel strands as templates. (2) Free DNA nucleotides pair by complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C) and hydrogen-bond into place. (3) DNA polymerase joins adjacent nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds, synthesising 5'→3' (leading continuous; lagging in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase). (4) Each daughter molecule has one original and one new strand. (5) Meselson-Stahl: E. coli grown in ¹⁵N then ¹⁴N gives, after one generation, DNA of intermediate density and, after two, half intermediate and half light - only semi-conservative replication predicts this banding, excluding conservative and dispersive models.
practiceQuestions: Describe the structure of DNA and explain how it is suited to its role of storing genetic information. (6 marks)
Describe transcription and state how pre-mRNA is processed in eukaryotes. (5 marks)
Describe translation and explain why the amino-acid sequence matches the gene. (5 marks)
Explain how a frameshift mutation affects the protein produced, contrasting it with a substitution. (4 marks)
Explain the features of the genetic code that make genetic engineering between species possible. (3 marks)
DNA polymerase can only synthesise DNA in the 5'→3' direction. Explain how the lagging strand is replicated. (3 marks)

topics.title: Gene Expression and Technology
learningObjectives: Explain how transcription factors, oestrogen and siRNA control gene expression (AQA 3.8.2.1-3.8.2.2; OCR 6.1.1)
Describe epigenetic control: DNA methylation and histone acetylation, and the epigenome (AQA 3.8.2.2; OCR 6.1.1)
Distinguish totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells and describe their sources and uses (AQA 3.8.2.2; OCR 6.1.1)
Describe making recombinant DNA: reverse transcriptase, restriction endonucleases, DNA ligase, vectors and marker genes (AQA 3.8.4.1-3.8.4.2; OCR 6.1.3)
Detail PCR stages and explain gel electrophoresis, DNA probes and DNA sequencing (AQA 3.8.4.3-3.8.4.4; OCR 6.1.3)
Describe genome projects, proteomics and evaluate ethical issues of gene technology and gene therapy
keyPoints: Transcription factors bind promoters: stimulatory or inhibitory; oestrogen binds ER in cytoplasm, complex acts as transcription factor
Epigenome: DNA methylation of CpG islands condenses chromatin (silences); histone acetylation loosens chromatin (activates); heritable without changing base sequence
siRNA: binds RISC, guides to complementary mRNA, cleaves it - prevents translation
Stem cells: totipotent (zygote) → pluripotent (blastocyst) → multipotent (bone marrow); iPS cells made by reprogramming with transcription factors
Recombinant DNA: reverse transcriptase (mRNA → cDNA), restriction endonucleases (sticky ends), DNA ligase (seals), plasmid vectors, marker genes
PCR: 95 °C denaturation, 55 °C annealing, 72 °C extension by Taq polymerase; doubles DNA each cycle
Gel electrophoresis: DNA fragments move to the anode; shorter fragments travel further - separates by size
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.8.4, 6 marks): Describe how the polymerase chain reaction is used to amplify a DNA fragment, including the role of primers and Taq polymerase.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 6 total): (1) DNA heated to ~95 °C - hydrogen bonds break, strands separate (denaturation). (2) Cooled to ~55 °C - primers bind complementarily to the 3' ends of the target sequence (annealing), providing a starting double-stranded segment for DNA synthesis and preventing the template strands re-annealing. (3) Heated to ~72 °C - Taq polymerase adds free nucleotides (dNTPs) to synthesise complementary strands (extension). (4) Taq polymerase is thermostable (from Thermus aquaticus) so is not denatured at 95 °C. (5) Each cycle doubles the quantity of DNA (exponential: 2ⁿ). (6) A thermal cycler automates the repeated temperature cycles; after ~30 cycles, ~1 billion copies are produced.
practiceQuestions: Explain how oestrogen stimulates transcription of target genes. (4 marks)
Explain how siRNA silences a specific target gene. (3 marks)
Distinguish totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells, and state one source of each. (4 marks)
Explain how restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase are used to insert a target gene into a plasmid vector. (5 marks)
Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments. (3 marks)
Explain why cDNA, rather than genomic DNA, is often used when transferring human genes to bacteria. (3 marks)

topics.title: Immunity
learningObjectives: Describe non-specific defences (barriers, inflammation, phagocytosis) and antigen presentation (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 4.1.1)
Describe cell-mediated immunity: T-helper and T-cytotoxic cells and clonal selection/expansion (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 4.1.1)
Describe humoral immunity: B cells, plasma cells, antibody structure and action (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 4.1.1)
Compare primary and secondary responses and explain vaccination and herd immunity (AQA 3.2.4; Edexcel A T6)
Distinguish active and passive immunity and describe monoclonal antibody uses (ELISA, pregnancy tests, targeted therapy)
Describe HIV structure and replication and explain antibiotic action and resistance (AQA 3.2.4/3.8; OCR 4.1.1)
keyPoints: Non-specific: skin, mucus, lysozyme, inflammation; phagocytosis: chemotaxis → phagosome → lysosome fusion → hydrolysis → antigen presentation
Cell-mediated: APC activates complementary T-helper cells → clonal expansion → T-cytotoxic cells kill infected/tumour cells with perforin
Humoral: T-helper activates B cells → clonal expansion → plasma cells (antibodies) + memory B cells
Antibody: 2 heavy + 2 light chains, disulfide bridges; variable region complementary to antigen; forms antigen-antibody complex; agglutination/opsonisation
Primary response: slow (clonal selection), antibody rises then falls; secondary: faster, stronger, longer (memory cells)
Vaccines: weakened/inactivated pathogens or antigens → active immunity; herd immunity protects the unvaccinated
HIV: RNA + reverse transcriptase in capsid; infects T-helper cells; reverse transcription → DNA → host transcription → viral proteins → budding
Antibiotics: target bacterial structures (cell wall, ribosomes); resistance via mutation + selection pressure
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.2.4, 6 marks): Describe how phagocytosis of a pathogen leads to activation of the specific immune response.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 6 total): (1) Phagocytes are attracted to the pathogen by chemicals it releases (chemotaxis). (2) The phagocyte engulfs the pathogen, enclosing it in a phagosome formed from the cell-surface membrane. (3) Lysosomes fuse with the phagosome, releasing hydrolytic enzymes. (4) The enzymes digest the pathogen; soluble products are absorbed. (5) The phagocyte becomes an antigen-presenting cell, displaying the pathogen's antigens on its cell-surface membrane. (6) The displayed antigens stimulate complementary T-helper cells (cell-mediated immunity), which activate specific B cells to clonally expand and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells (humoral immunity).
practiceQuestions: Describe the process of phagocytosis and explain how it leads to activation of the specific immune response. (6 marks)
Explain how the structure of an antibody is related to its function. (4 marks)
Compare the primary and secondary immune responses. (5 marks)
Explain how vaccination leads to immunity and why it protects the unvaccinated. (5 marks)
Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viruses but effective against bacteria. (4 marks)
Describe the structure of HIV and explain how it replicates in T-helper cells. (6 marks)

topics.title: Photosynthesis
learningObjectives: Describe chloroplast structure and photosynthetic pigments; interpret absorption and action spectra (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1)
Describe the light-dependent reaction: photolysis, electron transport chain, photophosphorylation and NADP reduction (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1)
Describe the light-independent reaction (Calvin cycle): RuBisCO, GP/TP, and the uses of triose phosphate (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1)
Explain limiting factors (light, CO₂, temperature) and interpret limiting-factor graphs (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1)
Describe the required practicals: chromatography of pigments (Rf values) and dehydrogenase activity (AQA RP7/RP8; OCR PAG11)
Apply the compensation point and agricultural optimisation of photosynthesis to exam scenarios
keyPoints: Chloroplast: thylakoid membranes (photosystems) stacked into grana; stroma contains Calvin-cycle enzymes; own DNA/ribosomes
Pigments: chlorophyll a (PSI/PSII reaction centre, blue-red absorption), chlorophyll b, carotenoids (accessory); absorption vs action spectra
LDR (thylakoid): photolysis 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂; ETC pumps H⁺ into thylakoid lumen; ATP synthase makes ATP; NADP + H⁺ + e⁻ → NADPH
Calvin cycle (stroma): CO₂ + RuBP → 2 GP (RuBisCO); GP reduced to TP (ATP + NADPH); 5/6 TP regenerates RuBP, 1/6 makes glucose
Limiting factors: light (plateaus - other factors limit), CO₂ (plateaus), temperature (enzyme kinetics); greenhouse optimisation
Practicals: chromatography of pigments with Rf values (AQA RP7); DCPIP dehydrogenase activity (AQA RP8); OCR PAG11
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.5.1, 5 marks): Describe how ATP and NADPH are produced in the light-dependent reaction of photosynthesis.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 5 total): (1) Light absorbed by chlorophyll a in photosystem II excites electrons to a higher energy level. (2) Electrons lost from chlorophyll are replaced by photolysis of water (2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂). (3) Electrons pass along an electron transport chain; energy released pumps H⁺ from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen, building a proton gradient. (4) H⁺ flow back through ATP synthase into the stroma drives photophosphorylation of ADP + Pi to ATP (chemiosmosis). (5) At photosystem I, electrons are re-excited and, with H⁺ from the stroma, reduce NADP to NADPH (NADP + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → NADPH).
practiceQuestions: Describe the light-independent reaction of photosynthesis and state the uses of triose phosphate. (6 marks)
Explain what happens to the concentrations of GP, TP and RuBP if a plant is placed in darkness. (4 marks)
Explain why oxygen is essential for aerobic ATP production. (3 marks)
A student runs a chromatogram of leaf pigments; a pigment moves 4.2 cm and the solvent front moves 8.4 cm. Calculate the Rf value and explain how Rf values are used. (3 marks)
Describe how the rate of photosynthesis can be investigated using DCPIP and isolated chloroplasts. (5 marks)
Explain how a commercial glasshouse increases the rate of photosynthesis, and evaluate the economics. (5 marks)

topics.title: Homeostasis and Nervous System
learningObjectives: Explain homeostasis principles: set points, receptors, effectors, negative and positive feedback (AQA 3.6.1; OCR 5.1.1)
Describe blood glucose control by insulin and glucagon, including cAMP second messengers; compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes (AQA 3.6.4.2; OCR 5.1.2)
Describe kidney structure and osmoregulation: ADH action and the loop of Henle counter-current multiplier (AQA 3.6.4.3; OCR 5.1.2)
Describe neurone structure, resting potential and action potential phases (AQA 3.6.2; OCR 5.3.1)
Explain synaptic transmission, summation and inhibition at cholinergic synapses (AQA 3.6.2; OCR 5.3.1)
Describe thermoregulation by the hypothalamus and interpret physiological control graphs
keyPoints: Homeostasis: set point → receptors → coordination (hormonal/nervous) → effectors → correction; negative feedback restores, positive amplifies
Blood glucose: insulin (β-cells, lowers - uptake, glycogenesis), glucagon (α-cells, raises - glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis via cAMP); T1: no insulin; T2: resistance
Kidney: nephron (Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct); loop of Henle: counter-current multiplier creates medullary gradient; ADH adds aquaporins in DCT/CD
Resting potential -70 mV (Na⁺/K⁺ pump, K⁺ leak); action potential: threshold -55 mV, depolarisation (Na⁺ in), repolarisation (K⁺ out), refractory period
Synapse: Ca²⁺ → vesicle fusion → ACh → postsynaptic receptors → depolarisation; acetylcholinesterase clears ACh; summation: temporal/spatial
Thermoregulation: thermoreceptors (skin + hypothalamus) → hypothalamic centre; cooling: vasodilation, sweating; warming: vasoconstriction, shivering, thyroxine/adrenaline
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.6.4.3, 5 marks): Describe how the loop of Henle creates a water potential gradient in the kidney medulla, and explain how ADH modifies urine production.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 5 total): (1) Descending limb: permeable to water, impermeable to ions - water leaves by osmosis into the medulla, concentrating the filtrate. (2) Ascending limb: impermeable to water - Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are actively transported out, diluting the filtrate and concentrating the medulla. (3) Counter-current flow (opposite directions) maintains and multiplies the gradient, deepest at the loop tip. (4) Low blood water potential: hypothalamic osmoreceptors → posterior pituitary releases ADH → ADH binds collecting duct receptors. (5) Aquaporins fuse with the membrane, increasing water permeability - more water reabsorbed, small volume of concentrated urine (negative feedback); high water potential suppresses ADH, producing dilute urine.
practiceQuestions: Describe the sequence of events in an action potential. (6 marks)
Explain how transmission occurs across a cholinergic synapse. (6 marks)
Describe how insulin and glucagon control blood glucose concentration. (6 marks)
Explain the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes. (4 marks)
Describe how the loop of Henle enables the production of concentrated urine. (5 marks)
Explain how the body responds to a rise in core temperature above 37 °C. (5 marks)

topics.title: Ecology and Ecosystems
learningObjectives: Define ecosystems, habitats and niches; describe trophic levels and food webs (AQA 3.5.3, 3.7.4; OCR 6.3.1)
Explain energy flow: GPP, NPP, ecological efficiency and pyramids of number/biomass/energy (AQA 3.5.3; OCR 6.3.1)
Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles including saprotrophs, fixation, nitrification and denitrification (AQA 3.5.4; OCR 6.3.1)
Explain population dynamics: growth curves, carrying capacity, limiting factors and predator-prey cycles (AQA 3.7.4; OCR 6.3.2)
Describe succession (primary/secondary, climax, deflected) and apply mark-release-recapture and quadrat sampling (AQA RP12; OCR PAG12)
Evaluate conservation strategies and human impacts: eutrophication, climate change, sustainable management
keyPoints: GPP = total energy fixed by producers; NPP = GPP − R; efficiency between trophic levels typically ~10%
Energy pyramids always upright; biomass/number pyramids can invert; energy lost as heat (respiration), faeces, urine, uneaten parts

Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decomposition, ocean uptake; Nitrogen: fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), assimilation, denitrification (Pseudomonas)
Growth curve: lag, log, stationary, death; carrying capacity K set by limiting factors; predator-prey cycles lag and oscillate
Succession: pioneer → intermediate → climax; deflected succession (grazing/mowing) → plagioclimax
Eutrophication: nitrates/phosphates → algal bloom → light blocked → decomposition → O₂ depletion → dead zones
Sampling: quadrats (abundance, % cover, ACFOR), belt transects, mark-release-recapture (N = n₁n₂/n_marked)
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA-style (3.7.4, 6 marks): Explain how succession occurs on bare rock, and how human activity can deflect it.
topics.modelAnswer: Model answer logic (1 mark per point, 6 total): (1) Pioneer species (lichens, mosses) colonise bare rock - adapted to harsh conditions (drought, low nutrients). (2) Pioneers die and are decomposed by saprotrophs, building a thin soil that retains water and nutrients. (3) Each stage modifies the environment, enabling the next: grasses then shrubs then trees colonise, outcompeting earlier species by growing taller and shading them. (4) Biodiversity and biomass rise through succession. (5) A climax community forms - stable, in equilibrium with the climate (e.g. woodland). (6) Deflected succession: human activity such as grazing, mowing or burning halts succession, maintaining a plagioclimax (e.g. grassland); if stopped, succession resumes toward the climax.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish between gross primary productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP), and state the equation linking them. (3 marks)
Explain why only about 10% of energy is transferred between trophic levels. (4 marks)
Describe the role of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle. (6 marks)
A scientist captures 40 mice, marks and releases them; a week later she captures 60, of which 12 are marked. Estimate the population and state two assumptions of the method. (3 marks)
Explain the sequence of events leading to eutrophication. (5 marks)
Describe a logistic (S-shaped) population growth curve and explain what determines the carrying capacity. (5 marks)

topics.title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
learningObjectives: Describe subatomic particles and use atomic number and mass number to deduce numbers of each particle
Define isotopes and calculate relative atomic mass from mass spectra of elements

topics.exampleQuestion: The first ionisation energies of magnesium and aluminium are 738 and 578 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium despite aluminium having a higher nuclear charge.
topics.modelAnswer: Aluminium's outer electron is in the 3p sub-shell ([Ne]3s²3p¹) whereas magnesium's is in the 3s sub-shell ([Ne]3s²). The 3p orbital is higher in energy and slightly further from the nucleus than 3s, and the 3s² pair shields the 3p electron. This makes the outer electron in aluminium easier to remove, outweighing the extra proton, so less energy is needed (578 vs 738 kJ mol⁻¹). Mark points: identify sub-shells; state 3p higher in energy/greater distance; state shielding; conclude easier removal. (AQA 7405 3.1.1.6; OCR 3.1.1.1)

topics.exampleQuestion: Explain why H₂O has a much higher boiling point than H₂S despite H₂S having a higher relative molecular mass.
topics.modelAnswer: H₂O molecules form hydrogen bonds: O is small and highly electronegative, leaving the H strongly δ+ and exposing lone pairs, so each molecule attracts neighbouring molecules strongly. H₂S has only permanent dipole-dipole and London forces (S is larger and less electronegative). Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than the other IMFs, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules — hence water boils at 100 °C while H₂S boils at −60 °C. Mark points: name hydrogen bonding; conditions (H on O, lone pair); compare with H₂S IMFs; energy-to-separate link. (AQA 3.1.3.10-3.1.3.11)

topics.exampleQuestion: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Predict and explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of ammonia of (a) increasing pressure, (b) increasing temperature, (c) adding an iron catalyst.
topics.modelAnswer: (a) 4 mol gas on the left → 2 mol on the right; increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles, so yield increases. (b) The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating shifts equilibrium in the endothermic (reverse) direction — yield falls. (c) A catalyst lowers Ea and speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the yield/position is unchanged. Mark points: mole count comparison; Le Chatelier reasoning; exothermic direction logic; catalyst has no effect on position. (AQA 3.1.6.1-3.1.6.2; OCR 5.1.2)

topics.exampleQuestion: Calculate the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.20 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵) and 0.15 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate, and explain how the pH changes when a small amount of dilute HCl is added.
topics.modelAnswer: [H⁺] = Ka × ([HA]/[A⁻]) = (1.74 × 10⁻⁵) × (0.20/0.15) = 2.32 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³; pH = −log₁₀(2.32 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.63. On adding HCl: the added H⁺ reacts with the ethanoate reservoir — CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH; the equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ shifts left, removing most of the added H⁺, so pH changes only slightly (as long as the CH₃COO⁻ reservoir remains large). Mark points: buffer equation; correct [H⁺]; pH with units-free value; buffer action equation; equilibrium shift.

topics.exampleQuestion: State and explain the trend in reactivity of the Group 2 metals down the group, and predict what you would observe when barium is added to cold water.
topics.modelAnswer: Reactivity increases down the group. Down the group each element has an extra full inner shell, so atomic radius and shielding both increase and the first (and second) ionisation energies fall — the two outer s electrons are lost more easily, so the metals react more readily. With barium in cold water: reacts vigorously, fizzing as hydrogen gas is released, and the solution becomes alkaline (Ba(OH)₂ is soluble): Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂. Mark points: trend stated; extra shell/shielding; ionisation energy decrease; observation with equation. (AQA 3.2.2.1-3.2.2.2; OCR 3.1.2.1)

topics.exampleQuestion: Propose a mechanism for the reaction of 2-methylpropene with HBr and explain the major product.
topics.modelAnswer: Electrophilic addition. Step 1: the π electron pair forms a bond to the H of H–Br while the H–Br bond breaks heterolytically (both electrons to Br) — curly arrow from the π bond to H and from the H–Br bond to Br. Step 2: the carbocation forms on the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) — a tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups — rather than a primary carbocation. Step 3: the Br⁻ lone pair attacks the positive carbon forming the C–Br bond. Product: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (major). Mark points: correct heterolytic fission; carbocation on tertiary carbon; justification by carbocation stability; curly-arrow description. (AQA 3.3.3.1-3.3.3.2)

topics.exampleQuestion: Identify C₃H₆O₂ showing IR absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ and a broad band 2500-3300 cm⁻¹, and ¹H NMR with a triplet at δ 1.1 (3H), a quartet at δ 2.4 (2H) and a singlet at δ 11.5 (1H).
topics.modelAnswer: 1. IR: 1715 cm⁻¹ (C=O) plus very broad 2500-3300 cm⁻¹ (carboxylic acid O-H) → carboxylic acid (-COOH). 2. ¹H NMR: δ 11.5 singlet is the -COOH proton (acid range, singlet because exchange prevents splitting). 3. Triplet δ 1.1 (3H) and quartet δ 2.4 (2H) indicate an ethyl group CH₃CH₂- (triplet: CH₃ split by 2 H on adjacent C; quartet: CH₂ split by 3 H). Structure: propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH. Mark points: identify functional groups from IR; assign -COOH proton; deduce ethyl group from splitting and integration; correct final structure consistent with formula.

topics.exampleQuestion: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of ethanoic acid of unknown concentration required a mean titre of 22.30 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH for neutralisation (1:1 ratio). Calculate the concentration of the ethanoic acid and state the indicator that should be used, justifying your choice.
topics.modelAnswer: Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 22.30/1000 = 2.23 × 10⁻³ mol. Ratio 1:1, so moles CH₃COOH in 25.0 cm³ = 2.23 × 10⁻³ mol. [CH₃COOH] = 2.23 × 10⁻³ × 1000/25.0 = 0.0892 mol dm⁻³. Indicator: phenolphthalein — weak acid-strong base titration, so the vertical section of the curve lies above 7 (equivalence pH > 7 from hydrolysis of the ethanoate salt); phenolphthalein's range 8.3-10.0 falls within it, whereas methyl orange (3.1-4.4) changes colour well before the equivalence point. Mark points: moles of titrant; correct ratio; concentration with units; indicator named; justification via curve shape.

keyPoints: SUVAT: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, s = ½(u+v)t -- only for constant a

Momentum p = mv; Impulse J = FDeltat = Deltap; Conservation: Σp_before = Σp_after (isolated system)
Work W = F·s = Fs cos θ; KE = ½mv^2; GPE = mgh; Elastic PE = ½kx^2; Power = W/t = Fv
Projectiles: horizontal v constant, vertical a = -g; range = u^2sin2θ/g, max height = u^2sin^2θ/(2g)
Circular: a = v^2/r = ω^2r, F = mv^2/r = mω^2r, ω = 2pi/T = 2pif, v = ωr
Moments: M = F x d (perpendicular distance); Couple: two equal/opposite forces separated by d
Equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0; Centre of mass: weighted mean of positions
Hooke: F = kx (within limit of proportionality); EPE = ½kx^2 = ½Fx
topics.exampleQuestion: A 0.5 kg ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30 deg  to horizontal. Find maximum height, range, and speed at impact
topics.modelAnswer: uₓ = 20cos30 deg  = 10sqrt3 ≈ 17.32 m/s; uᵧ = 20sin30 deg  = 10 m/s. Max height: vᵧ^2 = uᵧ^2 - 2gh -> 0 = 100 - 19.6h -> h = 5.10 m. Time of flight: t = 2uᵧ/g = 20/9.8 = 2.04 s. Range = uₓ x t = 17.32 x 2.04 = 35.3 m. At impact: vᵧ = -10 m/s, v = sqrt(17.32^2 + 10^2) = 20 m/s

topics.exampleQuestion: Write a function that reads a file of integers and returns the median
topics.modelAnswer:
def median_from_file(filename):
    with open(filename) as f:
        nums = sorted(int(line.strip()) for line in f if line.strip())
    n = len(nums)
    if n == 0: return None
    mid = n // 2
    return nums[mid] if n % 2 else (nums[mid-1] + nums[mid]) / 2
