1. Outline and evaluate the contribution of action theories to our understanding of society. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two similarities between functionalist and Marxist theory. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 — accurate knowledge of Weber (verstehen, four action types), symbolic interactionism (Becker, Goffman), phenomenology (Schutz, typifications), ethnomethodology (Garfinkel's breaching experiments) and Giddens' structuration. AO2 — apply each to social topics (labelling in education and crime, everyday interaction). AO3 — evaluate with structuralist rebuttals (class and poverty constrain regardless of meaning), Archer's critique of structuration as too abstract, empirical successes (Garfinkel 1967; Becker 1963), and a reached judgement that action theories best explain micro-processes but need structural context. Q2 (10 marks): two developed similarities with application, e.g. both are structural theories explaining behaviour through society shaping individuals; both make socialisation central to maintaining order; both are macro, modernist claims to general truths. Developed application only — no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and analyse two ways in which action theories differ from structural theories. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate functionalist explanations of social order. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two criticisms Marxism makes of functionalism. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that patriarchy is the most important form of inequality in society. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons why postmodernists reject meta-narratives. [10 marks]

topics.title: Research Methods
learningObjectives: Classify research data as quantitative/qualitative and primary/secondary, and match methods to positivism or interpretivism (AQA 4.1.3.1-3)
Outline the practical, ethical and theoretical strengths and limitations of each main method (AQA 4.1.3.1)
Describe the research process from aim to report, including stratified random sampling, quota sampling and pilot studies (AQA 4.1.3.4)
Apply theoretical, practical and ethical considerations to the choice of topic, method and conduct of research (AQA 4.1.3.5)
Evaluate positivism and interpretivism with named studies and methodological pluralism (AO3)
Deploy methods knowledge in 10-mark, 20-mark and 30-mark answers across AQA Papers 1 and 3 and OCR H580/02
keyPoints: Positivism seeks reliable, representative data for causal laws (Durkheim); interpretivism seeks valid, authentic data for meanings (Weber).
Questionnaires and official statistics suit positivists; unstructured interviews and participant observation suit interpretivists.
Sampling: random, systematic, stratified random, quota, snowball, opportunity — probability techniques need a sampling frame.
Ethics: informed consent, deception, confidentiality, harm, right to withdraw (BSA ethical guidelines).
PET/E rule: every method evaluation must name a practical constraint, an ethical issue or a theoretical position — bare lists earn little credit.
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Assess the usefulness of participant observation for investigating crime and deviance. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two advantages of using official statistics in sociological research. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 — accurate knowledge of participant observation (overt/covert, gaining trust, verstehen) plus the positivism-interpretivism context. AO2 — apply to crime: access to hidden subcultures and motives no survey reaches (Venkatesh 2008; Winlow 2001), but danger, time and gatekeeper problems in researching criminals. AO3 — strengths: high validity (Humphreys 1970 accessed behaviour impossible to study otherwise); limitations: unrepresentative, unreliable, ethical costs of covert work, researcher effects (going native); balance against positivist alternatives (official statistics and the CSEW expose only part of the dark figure). Judgement: useful for meanings and hidden worlds, inadequate alone for extent and distribution. Q2 (10 marks): two developed advantages with application only — e.g. large-scale and representative, allowing generalisation and trends over time (birth rates since 1900); free and quick to access, enabling comparisons between groups; reliable because standardised, so replicable (Durkheim's suicide study 1897). Development only — no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and analyse two advantages of using official statistics in sociological research. [10 marks]
Assess the usefulness of unstructured interviews for investigating domestic violence. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons why covert participant observation may be ethically problematic. [10 marks]
Assess the claim that sociological research can never be value-free. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons why a stratified random sample may improve representativeness. [10 marks]
Assess the usefulness of participant observation for investigating crime and deviance. [30 marks]

topics.title: Methods in Context and Theory
learningObjectives: Apply practical, ethical and theoretical (PET) evaluation to questionnaires, interviews, observations and documents in education settings (AQA 4.1.4; OCR H580/02)
Write the 20-mark methods in context answer with sustained application to the named education topic (AQA Paper 1 Q5: AO1 + AO2 only)
Anticipate education-specific research problems: classroom access, gatekeepers, safeguarding, the Hawthorne effect and teacher-pupil power
Deploy education research studies (Willis, Lacey, Ball, Mac an Ghaill, Gillborn and Youdell) as applied evidence
Link method choice to positivism versus interpretivism and to debates over value freedom (AQA 4.4)
Plan 30-mark theory-and-methods essays on sociology as a science and value freedom (AQA 7192 Paper 3; synoptic theory essays on OCR H580/03)
keyPoints: AQA methods in context (Paper 1 Q5): 20 marks, AO1 + AO2 only — sustained application to the named education topic is what separates levels (AQA 4.1.4).
Every PET point must be APPLIED: 'registers give questionnaires a complete sampling frame' beats a generic list of strengths.
Education-specific strengths: registers as sampling frames, fixed timetables easing access, anonymous surveys drawing out honest pupil answers.
Education-specific limitations: gatekeepers (headteacher, DfE, parents), DBS and safeguarding checks, strong Hawthorne effect with children, teacher-pupil power distorting data.

Studies to deploy: Willis (1977) group interviews with the lads; Lacey (1970) Hightown Grammar; Ball (1981) Beachside; Mac an Ghaill (1988) teacher-researcher; Gillborn and Youdell (2000) Rationing Education.
30-mark theory-and-methods essays (AQA 4.4): positivism versus interpretivism underpins method choice; value freedom (Weber, Becker, Gouldner) supplies the evaluation.
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Item C reports research on anti-school subcultures in a comprehensive school. Applying material from the item and your wider sociological knowledge, evaluate the strengths and limitations of using non-participant observation to investigate pupil subcultures in schools. [20 marks]
2. Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to investigate class differences in educational achievement. [20 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (20 marks): AO1 — method knowledge: non-participant observation means the researcher watches classroom events without joining in; can be overt or covert. AO2 (the differentiator — every point applied to schools and subcultures): access — headteacher permission, DBS checks and staff cooperation are needed, but fixed timetables make classrooms visible and easy to schedule (practical strength); Hawthorne effect — pupils perform for a visible adult, so subcultures may go underground (Woods 1979), threatening validity (theoretical limitation); unrepresentative single school, unrepeatable so unreliable, no generalisation to schools nationally (theoretical limitation); watching interaction directly captures subculture formation — differentiation and polarisation (Lacey 1970; Ball 1981) — which questionnaires cannot reach (theoretical strength); covert variants breach consent and safeguarding with children, rarely ethical (ethical limitation). PET structure required: 3-4 paragraphs each pairing a strength with a limitation, sustained application throughout. Conclusion: the validity of watching subcultures form outweighs access and ethics costs for a small-scale study, but generalisation to pupils nationally is weak. Q2 (20 marks): official statistics — practical: free, up-to-date, whole-cohort coverage, representative (strength); ethical: no consent issues at aggregate level, but identifiable individuals risk exposure (limitation); theoretical: reliable and positivist, enabling hypothesis-testing on class and attainment, BUT socially constructed (Cicourel), performativity-distorted (Ball 2003) and hiding off-rolling and internal exclusions (Gillborn and Youdell 2000), and they ignore meanings (interpretivist limitation). Judgement: strong for measuring patterns, weak for explaining them.
practiceQuestions: Applying material from the item and your knowledge, evaluate the strengths and limitations of using questionnaires to investigate pupils' attitudes towards education. [20 marks]
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to investigate teachers' use of labelling. [20 marks]
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using covert participant observation to investigate pupil subcultures. [20 marks]
Outline and explain two ethical problems of using covert observation to investigate classroom behaviour. [10 marks]
Evaluate the view that sociology can and should be value-free. [30 marks]

topics.title: Families and Households
learningObjectives: Set out functionalist, Marxist, feminist and personal life accounts of the family with named theorists (AQA 4.2.2.1)
Explain the family's relationship to social structure, the economy and state policies (AQA 4.2.2.2)
Describe changing patterns of marriage, cohabitation, separation, divorce and child-bearing and evaluate the explanations (AQA 4.2.2.3)
Analyse gender roles, domestic labour and power relationships, including domestic violence (AQA 4.2.2.4)
Evaluate the nature of childhood and its changing status in family and society (AQA 4.2.2.5)
Interpret UK demographic trends since 1900 — birth rates, death rates, ageing, migration — and link them to globalisation (AQA 4.2.2.6)
keyPoints: Functionalist: Murdock (1949, four functions), Parsons (primary socialisation, stabilisation of adult personalities, functional fit); New Right update — Murray, Marsland.
Marxist: Engels (1884, inheritance of property), Zaretsky (1976, unit of consumption and haven), Ansley (1972, women as 'takers of shit').
Changing patterns: later and fewer marriages, rising cohabitation, around 40% of marriages ending in divorce, births outside marriage at about half of all births (ONS).
Domestic labour: Oakley (1974), Boulton (1983), Gershuny (1994) lagged adaptation, Duncombe and Marsden (1995) triple shift, Dobash and Dobash (1980) violence.
Childhood: Aries (1960) the invention of childhood, Postman (1994) its disappearance, Palmer (2006) toxic childhood; March of progress vs conflict view.
Demography: birth rate fallen from about 28 to about 11 per 1,000 since 1900; ageing population (Hirsch 2005); record net migration reshaping families.
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Outline and evaluate the view that the family is beneficial for all its members. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two reasons for the decline in the marriage rate. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 — functionalism (Murdock 1949 four functions; Parsons' warm bath), Marxism (Engels, Zaretsky, Ansley), feminism (Delphy and Leonard), personal life (Smart 2007). AO2 — apply to socialisation, domestic labour, childhood, domestic violence. AO3 — functionalism ignores the dark side (Dobash and Dobash 1980; Oakley 1974 dissatisfaction); Marxists see the family serving capitalism not members; radical feminists see it serving men; personal life shows 'benefit' depends on the relationship, and some members (children, women) do worse than others. Judgement: the family benefits members unevenly — perspective-dependent. Q2 (10 marks): two developed reasons, e.g. secularisation and declining stigma (Wilson; Weeks 1999) — marriage loses religious status, cohabitation normalised; women's economic independence (Wilkinson 1994 'genderquake') — less need to marry for financial security; rising expectations (Fletcher 1966). Developed application only — no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and analyse two functions the family performs for society. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the Marxist view that the family serves capitalism. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons for the rise in cohabitation. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that childhood is improving (the March of Progress view). [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two ways in which domestic labour remains unequal. [10 marks]

topics.title: Education
learningObjectives: Set out functionalist, Marxist and feminist views of the role of the education system (AQA 4.1.1.1)
Explain class differences in achievement through external (material and cultural) and internal factors (AQA 4.1.1.2)
Explain ethnic and gender differences in achievement with named studies and dates (AQA 4.1.1.3-4)
Analyse relationships and processes within schools: labelling, streaming, pupil subcultures and pupil identities (AQA 4.1.1.5)
Evaluate the significance of educational policies from 1944 to the present, including marketisation, parentocracy, privatisation and globalisation of policy (AQA 4.1.1.6)
Deploy education content in 10- and 30-mark essays and in the Methods in Context question (AQA 4.1.2)
keyPoints: Functionalist: Durkheim (school as society in miniature), Parsons (1961, bridge and meritocracy), Davis and Moore (1945, role allocation).
Marxist: Bowles and Gintis (1976, correspondence principle), Althusser (1971, ISA), Willis (1977, lads resist).
Class — external: material deprivation (Smith and Noble 1995), cultural capital (Bourdieu 1984; Sullivan 2001); internal: labelling (Becker), streaming (Lacey 1970, Ball 1981).
Ethnic: Gillborn and Youdell (2000, educational triage), Coard (1971), Fuller (1984), Mirza (1997), institutional racism (Gillborn 2008).
Gender: girls' improvement (Gorard et al 2001; Sharpe 1994), boys' underachievement (Mitsos and Browne 1998), laddish subcultures (Sewell).
Policy: 1944 tripartite, comprehensives, 1988 ERA marketisation, parentocracy (Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz 1994), privatisation (Ball and Youdell 2008), PISA policy borrowing (Ball 2008).
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Outline and evaluate the view that working-class underachievement in education is the result of factors inside school. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two ways in which marketisation policies have affected schools. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 — internal factors: labelling (Becker 1971 ideal pupil), self-fulfilling prophecy (Rosenthal and Jacobson 1968), streaming and subcultures (Hargreaves 1967; Lacey 1970; Ball 1981), pupil identities (Archer et al 2010). AO2 — apply each to working-class pupils specifically. AO3 — external factors matter: material deprivation (Tanner et al 2003; Flaherty 2004) and cultural capital (Bourdieu 1984; Sullivan 2001) explain gaps in-school processes cannot; labels reflect class power, not individual teacher bias (Marxism); many pupils resist labels (Fuller 1984). Judgement: internal processes matter but interact with out-of-school causes — neither alone explains underachievement. Q2 (10 marks): two developed effects, e.g. formula funding and league tables created competition and a claimed parentocracy (David), raising standards where schools compete (Chubb and Moe 1990); cream-skimming and silt-shifting (Bartlett 1993) let successful schools select high-achievers, widening inequality (Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz 1994 myth of parentocracy). Developed application only — no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and analyse two functions of the education system. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the functionalist view that education is meritocratic. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two ways in which labelling may affect pupils' achievement. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that ethnic differences in achievement are mainly caused by factors within schools. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons why girls now outperform boys in education. [10 marks]

topics.title: Crime and Deviance
learningObjectives: Set out functionalist, strain and subcultural theories of crime and deviance with named theorists (AQA 4.3.1.1)
Explain interactionist and labelling theory, including secondary deviance and the dark figure (AQA 4.3.1.2)
Analyse the social distribution of crime by class, gender, ethnicity, age and locality, including recent patterns (AQA 4.3.1.4)
Evaluate explanations of globalisation and crime, green crime, state crime and the media-crime relationship (AQA 4.3.1.5)
Assess crime control, prevention and punishment, victims, and the role of the criminal justice system (AQA 4.3.1.6)
Deploy crime content in 10- and 30-mark essays and Methods in Context (AQA 4.3.2; 4.4.4)
keyPoints: Durkheim: crime is inevitable and universal; functions include boundary maintenance, adaptation and change; too much crime produces anomie.

Merton (1938): five adaptations to strain — conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism, rebellion; Cohen (1955) status frustration; Cloward and Ohlin (1960) criminal, conflict, retreatist subcultures; Miller (1958) focal concerns; Matza (1964) drift.
Interactionist: Becker (1963) labelling, Lemert (1951) secondary deviance, Cicourel (1968) negotiated justice, Braithwaite (1992) reintegrative shaming.
Distribution: dark figure — victim surveys (CSEW) reveal unrecorded crime; self-reports show smaller gender and ethnic gaps (Graham and Bowling 1995; Sharp and Budd 2005).
Global: Hobbs and Dunningham (1998) glocal crime, Castells (1998), Beck (1992) risk society; green crime (South 1998; White 2008); state crime (Green and Ward 2004).
Control: situational prevention (Clarke 1997), broken windows (Wilson and Kelling 1982), left realism (Lea and Young 1984), Foucault (1977) panopticon, Garland (2001) culture of control.
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Outline and evaluate interactionist explanations of crime and deviance. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two reasons why the official statistics may not give an accurate picture of crime. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 — Becker (1963) labelling and moral entrepreneurs; Lemert (1951) primary and secondary deviance; Cicourel (1968) typifications in juvenile justice; Braithwaite (1992) reintegrative shaming; Young (1971) hippies. AO2 — apply to police discretion, youth deviance and the construction of statistics. AO3 — deterministic: many resist labels (Fuller 1984); ignores the origins of primary deviance; structural alternatives (Merton's strain; Marxism — labels reflect class power); realists argue real differences exist. Judgement: interactionism best explains reaction and the dark figure, but needs structural context. Q2 (10 marks): two developed reasons — e.g. unreported crime (victims reluctant for fear, stigma or distrust), so the dark figure is missed (CSEW victim surveys reveal it); police recording practices and changed definitions inflate or deflate recorded crime (Farrington and Dowds 1986). Development only — no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and analyse two ways in which crime can be functional for society. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate Merton's strain theory of crime. [30 marks]
Outline and evaluate sociological explanations of female crime. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons why ethnic minorities may appear more criminal in official statistics. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the right realist view that crime is best prevented through situational crime prevention. [30 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that state crime is best defined through human rights. [30 marks]

topics.title: Beliefs in Society
learningObjectives: Compare religion, science and ideology as worldviews, including Popper's falsification and Horton's open/closed systems (AQA 4.2.1)
Set out Durkheim's functionalism, Weber's theodicy and rationalisation, and Marx's account of religion as ideology, with evaluation
Classify religious organisations using Troeltsch and Stark & Bainbridge, and explain the church-sect trajectory
Assess secularisation evidence (Wilson, Bruce) against supply-side and cultural-defence counter-arguments
Explain the postmodernist account of religion (Lyon, Davie) and theories of fundamentalism (Giddens, Bruce)
Deploy named studies and reached judgements in 10- and 30-mark answers (AO1/AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Durkheim (1912): religion = separation of sacred and profane; totemism shows society worshipping itself; religion has cognitive and integrative functions. Critique: Worsley - no sharp sacred/profane split in some tribes; works best in small-scale societies.

Weber (1905): Calvinist predestination and this-worldly asceticism produced the 'Protestant ethic', fuelling capitalism; rationalisation disenchant the world. Critique: capitalism predates Calvinism in Catholic Italy; multi-causal.

Marx: religion as ruling-class ideology, 'opium of the people'; Lenin's 'spiritual gin'. Critique: ignores the meaning religion gives the oppressed (Weber); religion can inspire resistance (liberation theology; MLK).

Typologies: Troeltsch (church, sect), Niebuhr (denomination), Stark & Bainbridge (audience/client/cultic-movement cults; sects from schism). Critique: ideal types that blur in reality (e.g. Mormonism fits no box).

Secularisation FOR: Wilson (contagion), Bruce (technological worldview; decline of community), attendance fall from ~40% (1851) to ~5-10%. AGAINST: Davie (belief without belonging), religious economy (America), cultural defence and transition (Bruce), Beckford - unsociological meta-concept.

Postmodernity: Lyon (Jesus in Disneyland; disembedding), Hervieu-Leger (spiritual shopping, pilgrims/converts). Fundamentalism: Giddens (defensive response to modernity; cosmopolitanism vs fundamentalism), Bruce (product of modernity).
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Outline and evaluate the view that secularisation is taking place in Britain today. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two explanations for the growth of new religious movements. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 - define secularisation (Wilson), set out the case: Bruce's technological worldview and decline of community, structural differentiation, rationalisation (Weber), and the statistics - attendance falling from ~40% (1851) to ~5-10%, collapsing baptisms and church weddings, secularisation from within (softened doctrine). AO2 - apply each point to British religious life and named institutions. AO3 - evaluate against Davie's belief without belonging, the religious economy (America; Stark & Bainbridge), cultural defence and cultural transition (Bruce's own concessions), Beckford's meta-concept critique, and postmodern transformation (Lyon; Hervieu-Leger). Reach a weighed judgement: institutional secularisation in mainstream churches is real, but belief, demand and global religion complicate the claim - never 'both views have merit'. Q2 (10 marks): two developed explanations with application, e.g. relative deprivation - sects offer compensators for rewards the world denies (Stark & Bainbridge); individualisation - NRMs as consumer products answering personalised spiritual needs (Wallis; Lyon). Developed application only - no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and analyse two functions religion performs for society. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the Marxist view that religion is ideological. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two differences between churches and sects. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that religion in a postmodern society is a matter of consumption. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two reasons why fundamentalism has grown. [10 marks]

topics.title: Social Stratification and Class
learningObjectives: Distinguish the four historical forms of stratification (slavery, caste, estate, class) and class/status/party as Weber's three dimensions (AQA 4.3.1)
Set out Marxist (bourgeoisie/proletariat), functionalist (Davis & Moore) and feminist accounts of stratification, with evaluation
Explain how class is measured (NS-SEC, Registrar-General) and the problems with occupational measurement
Apply Weber's concept of life chances to evidence on health, education, wealth and deprivation
Analyse patterns and explanations of social mobility using Goldthorpe's studies, including feminist and postmodern critiques
Reach weighed judgements between competing explanations in 10- and 30-mark answers (AO1/AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Four forms of stratification: slavery (ownership of persons), caste (birth-ascribed, closed, Hindu varna), estate (feudal, law-defined) and class (achieved, open, market-based) - only class is the modern form.

Weber: class is market position, not ownership alone; status can cut across class (black doctors, poor aristocrats); party adds political power. Critique: 'class, status and party' overlap and are hard to operationalise separately.

Marx: two-class polarisation, exploitation, ruling-class ideology; neo-Marxists (Wright's contradictory class locations; Gramsci's hegemony) update the picture. Critique: polarisation never happened - middle class grew (Weber; 'embourgeoisement').

Functionalist: Davis & Moore (1945) role allocation - stratification is functionally necessary. Critique: Tumin (1953) - circular, ignores inherited wealth and blocked opportunity, rewards reflect power not functional importance.

Feminist: stratification is gendered - Walby's six patriarchal structures; dual-systems theory (capitalism + patriarchy); vertical segregation and the glass ceiling; feminist critique of NS-SEC for scoring women by men's jobs.

Life chances: Black Report (1980) class gradients in health; wealth gaps; Townsend's relative deprivation. Postmodern claim (Pakulski & Waters; Bauman) that class is dead is countered by Westergaard - inequality is still class-shaped.

Goldthorpe (1972 Oxford Mobility Study, replicated 1992; Sutton Trust 2019): high absolute mobility from white-collar expansion ('upward drift') but stable relative rates - class of origin still shapes destination; long-range 'unjustified' upward mobility into the service class.
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Outline and evaluate the view that social class remains the most important source of inequality in Britain today. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two reasons why rates of social mobility have changed. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 - define stratification; set out Weber's class/status/party, Marxist polarisation (bourgeoisie/proletariat; ideology), functionalist role allocation (Davis & Moore), and feminist gendered stratification (Walby). AO2 - apply to NS-SEC measurement, life-chance evidence (Black Report 1980; wealth and education gaps; Townsend), and mobility patterns (Goldthorpe 1972/1992; Sutton Trust 2019). AO3 - evaluate: Weber's status dimension cuts across class (intersectionality), feminists argue patriarchy rivals class (Walby; dual systems), postmodernists claim class is dead (Pakulski & Waters; Bauman) countered by Westergaard; Tumin undermines Davis & Moore. Reach a weighed judgement - e.g. class remains the structural skeleton of inequality but operates now alongside gender, ethnicity and consumption. Q2 (10 marks): two developed reasons with application, e.g. (1) upward drift - service-class expansion created absolute mobility room at the top (Goldthorpe); (2) stable relative rates plus the glass ceiling - education reproduces origin (Boudon) and women's mobility is constrained (Stanworth 1984). Developed application only - no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and evaluate functionalist explanations of social stratification. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two differences between Marxist and Weberian accounts of class. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that social mobility has increased in Britain. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two problems with measuring social class by occupation. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that stratification is gendered as well as classed. [30 marks]

topics.title: Media
learningObjectives: Explain the growth of new media, Jenkins' convergence and participatory culture, and the digital divide (AQA 4.7.1)
Set out Marxist and hegemonic accounts of ownership and control (Murdock & Golding, Miliband, Gramsci, Herman & Chomsky) against pluralism
Analyse representations of gender, ethnicity and age with named concepts (symbolic annihilation, male gaze, tokenism)
Compare audience-effect models: hypodermic syringe, two-step flow, uses and gratifications, encoding/decoding
Explain moral panics (Cohen 1972), deviancy amplification and their links to labelling theory
Assess globalisation debates - cultural imperialism against hybridisation - and deploy reached judgements (AO1/AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: New media: Jenkins (convergence, participatory culture, 'fans as producers'); digital divide by age, class, geography ('digital underclass'). Critique: Cornford & Robbins - 'new' media is actually older media repackaged; commercial logics persist.

Ownership FOR control: Murdock & Golding - concentration and the profit motive skew content; Miliband - media transmit ruling-class ideology; Herman & Chomsky's five filters; Gramsci's hegemony. AGAINST: pluralism - competition, regulation (Ofcom), and Web 2.0 plurality disperse control.

Representations: gender - symbolic annihilation (Tuchman 1978), male gaze (Mulvey 1975), feminised beauty norms; ethnicity - negative stereotypes, tokenism, exclusion (Hall's 'inferential racism'; Gilroy on the 'war on terror'); age - children as innocent/victims, the elderly as frail or invisible (Carrigan & Szmigin).

Audience effects: hypodermic syringe (passive audiences) -> two-step flow (Katz & Lazarsfeld 1955, opinion leaders) -> uses and gratifications (active audiences; Blumler & McQuail) -> encoding/decoding (Hall 1973, negotiated and oppositional readings). Evidence: Bandura (1963) supports limited direct effects; Livingston/Gauntlett argue effects research understates audience activity.

Moral panics: Cohen (1972) mods and rockers - exaggeration, prediction, symbolisation; folk devils; deviancy amplification; linked to labelling (Becker 1963); 'amplification of deviance' now extends to social media.

Globalisation: cultural imperialism (US dominance; Sklair's culture-ideology of consumerism) vs hybridisation and the 'global village' (McLuhan); Ritzer's McDonaldisation; new media accelerate global flows and citizen journalism.
topics.exampleQuestion:
1. Outline and evaluate the view that the mass media play a key role in creating moral panics. [30 marks]
2. Outline and analyse two reasons why ownership of the media matters for the content they produce. [10 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Q1 (30 marks): AO1 - define moral panic (Cohen 1972); set out the process: exaggeration, prediction, symbolisation; folk devils; deviancy amplification; link to labelling (Becker 1963) and to moral entrepreneurs. AO2 - apply to mods and rockers (Cohen), to subsequent panics (youth subcultures, refugees, single mothers, social-media panics) and to the roles of police, courts and politicians as agents of control. AO3 - evaluate: McRobbie & Thornton (1995) - modern panics come with counter-panics and target-group responses; two-step flow and uses and gratifications show audiences negotiate rather than accept media inflation; pluralists note the media reflect real public fears as often as they create them; but the hypodermic syringe's laboratory evidence (Bandura 1963) and contemporary amplification through social media support media power. Reach a weighed judgement - e.g. media ignite and amplify panics, but audience interpretation and control agents decide whether they burn. Q2 (10 marks): two developed reasons with application, e.g. (1) concentration and the profit motive skew content towards elite interests (Murdock & Golding 1977); (2) hegemony and the five filters - advertising, sourcing and flak systematically produce elite-friendly news without conspiracy (Gramsci; Herman & Chomsky 1988). Developed application only - no extended evaluation required.
practiceQuestions: Outline and evaluate the pluralist view that media content reflects the choices of audiences. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two strengths of the uses and gratifications model. [10 marks]
Outline and evaluate the view that representations of gender in the media reinforce patriarchy. [30 marks]
Outline and analyse two features of a moral panic. [10 marks]
Outline and analyse two effects of media globalisation. [10 marks]

topics.title: Globalisation and Development
learningObjectives: Define globalisation and distinguish its economic (trade, TNCs, capital flows), political (IGOs, sovereignty) and cultural (Westernisation, hybridisation) dimensions (AQA 4.6.1)
Set out modernisation theory - Rostow's five stages - and its functionalist assumptions, with critiques of ethnocentrism and ignored colonialism
Evaluate dependency theory (Frank's development of underdevelopment) and world-systems theory (Wallerstein's core-periphery model)
Analyse aid, trade and TNCs with case examples (Shell in Nigeria, Rana Plaza, Foxconn) and evaluate the aid vs trade debate (Moyo vs Sachs)
Assess environmental consequences of global development: TNC pollution, deforestation, e-waste and unequal climate impacts
Deploy feminist perspectives on development (WID/GAD, feminisation of labour, Elson & Pearson) and postdevelopment critiques (Escobar)
Build 10- and 20-mark answers with reached judgements and synoptic links to modernisation and Marxist theory (AO1/AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Dimensions: economic (TNCs, trade, capital flows), political (WTO, IMF, World Bank, UN; eroded nation-state sovereignty), cultural (Westernisation/cultural imperialism - Sklair; hybridisation and glocalisation - Tomlinson). Held's typology: hyperglobalisers, sceptics, transformationalists.

Modernisation (Rostow 1960): five stages - traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption. Critique: ethnocentric, ignores colonial extraction, assumes one path; East Asian NICs developed under state direction, not Western values.

Dependency (Frank 1967): metropole-satellite chains extract surplus; 'development of underdevelopment'. Critique: ignores internal barriers (corruption, war) and cannot explain NIC escapes (South Korea, Taiwan).
World-systems (Wallerstein 1974): core, semi-periphery and periphery in one world economy; positions can shift (East Asia's rise) - the most critique-proof version of the Marxist account.

Aid vs trade: aid dependency, corruption and tied aid (Moyo, Dead Aid 2009) vs Sachs' targeted 'big push'; trade as long-run engine but unfair terms and commodity dependence; fair trade as a partial fix.

TNC cases: Shell in Nigeria (Ogoniland pollution, Ken Saro-Wiwa), Rana Plaza collapse 2013 (Primark supply chain), Foxconn/Apple labour conditions, Starbucks' tax avoidance - harm and benefit must be weighed, not asserted.

Environment: TNC pollution, Amazon deforestation for beef and soy, e-waste exported to Ghana and Nigeria, climate impacts falling hardest on those who contributed least; links to green and state crime (AQA 4.3.1.5).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that aid does more harm than good to developing countries. (AQA Paper 2, 20 marks; OCR H580/03 Section A sets a comparable source-based evaluation of globalisation and development claims.)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for the 20-marker (AO1/AO2/AO3): AO1 - define and set out: define aid (bilateral, multilateral, tied, NGO) and note that 'harm' and 'good' need spelling out - dependency, corruption and service cuts against investment, health gains and growth. AO2 - apply and analyse both sides. Harm case with named evidence: Moyo (Dead Aid 2009) - aid breeds dependency, fuels corruption and, via tied aid, benefits donors; case evidence: IMF structural adjustment cutting public services, food aid undermining local farmers. Benefit case: Sachs - targeted aid works (debt relief, vaccine programmes, Millennium Development Goals evidence); bottom-up NGO projects reach where states cannot. AO3 - evaluate: Moyo conflates all aid with its worst forms and ignores success cases; Sachs' 'big push' is contested (Easterly's planners vs searchers); aid effects depend on recipient governance - so the dichotomy is false. Judgement (required for the top band): aid is not inherently harmful, but tied, top-down aid without accountability tends to entrench dependency - the strongest answers weigh both sides against evidence, structure paragraphs as claim-evidence-evaluation, and close with a defended verdict rather than 'both views have merit'.
practiceQuestions: Outline and explain two economic dimensions of globalisation. [10 marks]
Evaluate the view that TNCs bring more harm than benefit to developing countries. [20 marks]
Evaluate modernisation theory as an explanation of global development. [20 marks]
Outline and explain two environmental consequences of global development. [10 marks]
Evaluate feminist views on the effects of global development on women. [20 marks]

The UK Constitution
learningObjectives: Describe the nature of the UK constitution — uncodified, unentrenched, unitary — and explain parliamentary sovereignty and the rule of law (AQA 3.1.1.1; Edexcel P2 1.1)
Identify the five sources of the constitution and illustrate each with statutes, cases or conventions (AO1)
Analyse the constitutional reforms of 1997–2010 and 2010 to the present, assessing their significance (AQA 3.1.1.2; Edexcel P2 1.2)
Explain the role and powers of the Scottish Parliament, Senedd and Northern Ireland Assembly (AQA 3.1.1.3; Edexcel P2 1.3)
Evaluate the impact of devolution on the UK, including the West Lothian Question and quasi-federalism (AO2/AO3)
Construct balanced arguments for and against codification and further reform (AQA 3.1.1.4; Edexcel P2 1.4)
keyPoints: Uncodified + unentrenched = flexible: any constitutional rule can be amended by a simple parliamentary majority.
Five sources: statute law, common law, conventions, works of authority, treaties.
Labour 1997–2010: devolution, HRA 1998, Lords Act 1999, FOI Act 2000, Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (Supreme Court 2009).
2010 onwards: FTPA 2011 (repealed 2022), Scotland Acts 2012/2016, EU Withdrawal Acts 2018/2020, DCPA 2022.
Miller II (2019): prorogation unlawful — courts willing to police the executive inside an uncodified constitution.
Devolution is asymmetric (Scotland strongest); England has no parliament — quasi-federal, not federal.
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA Paper 1: 'Analyse the arguments in favour of a codified constitution for the UK.' [25 marks] Edexcel Paper 2: 'Evaluate the view that the UK's constitution should be codified and entrenched.' (30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AQA 25 marks: AO1 12 / AO2 13): AO1 — accurate knowledge of the uncodified, unentrenched nature of the constitution; the amendment process (simple majority, no referendum required); examples of flexibility (devolution, HRA 1998, the FTPA's repeal in 2022). AO2 — developed arguments FOR codification: clarity and accessibility of the rules; stronger entrenchment of rights (contrast the HRA's s3/s4 with judicial enforcement in the USA); limiting executive power (Miller II showed the limits of courts policing conventions); democratic legitimacy. Then counter-arguments: flexibility allows rapid response to events; parliamentary sovereignty means any judicial ruling could be overridden; risk of judicial activism; 'if it ain't broke' — the constitution has adapted well (1997–2022 record). Conclusion: a supported judgement (e.g. codification is desirable in principle but politically unlikely, or flexibility is a strength rather than a weakness). Edexcel (30 marks) additionally requires: alternative viewpoints (codify vs keep uncodified, plus partial options such as a statutory Bill of Rights), contemporary examples since 1997, and a sustained final judgement that weights the evidence rather than listing both sides.
practiceQuestions: Explain the term 'uncodified constitution'. [5 marks]
Analyse the impact of devolution on the UK. [25 marks]
Evaluate the view that devolution has been the most significant constitutional reform since 1997. (30 marks)
Evaluate the view that the Human Rights Act 1998 has strengthened the protection of rights in the UK. (30 marks)
Analyse how the constitution has changed since 2010. [25 marks]

topics.title: Parliament
learningObjectives: Describe the structure and composition of the Commons and Lords, and explain Commons primacy (AQA 3.1.2.1; Edexcel P2 2.1)
Explain the functions of Parliament: legislation, scrutiny, representation, recruitment, deliberation and legitimacy (AQA 3.1.2.2; Edexcel P2 2.2)
Outline the stages of the legislative process and analyse how government and backbenchers shape bills (AQA 3.1.2.3; Edexcel P2 2.3)
Analyse the mechanisms of scrutiny — questions, select committees, debates and votes — and assess their effectiveness (AQA 3.1.2.2/3; Edexcel P2 2.4)
Evaluate how effectively Parliament holds the executive to account (AO2/AO3)
Evaluate arguments for and against a fully elected House of Lords (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Commons primacy: democratic mandate + Parliament Acts 1911/1949 — the Lords can delay and amend but not defeat (with rare exceptions).
Salisbury Convention: the Lords does not veto manifesto bills (tested by the Brexit amendments, 2017–19).
Functions: legislation, scrutiny, representation, recruitment of ministers, deliberation, legitimacy.
Scrutiny tools: PMQs, ministerial and urgent questions, departmental select committees (chairs elected since 2010), the Liaison Committee.
2019: May's record Commons defeats (three rejections of her Brexit deal) — the strongest modern evidence of Commons power.
Royal assent is a formality — last refused 1708; the Lords' veto was curtailed by the Parliament Acts.
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA Paper 1: 'Analyse the ways in which Parliament can hold the executive to account.' [25 marks] Edexcel Paper 2: 'Evaluate the view that select committees are the most effective means of holding the executive to account.' (30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AQA 25 marks: AO1 12 / AO2 13): AO1 — accurate coverage of scrutiny mechanisms: PMQs; ministerial and urgent questions; departmental select committees and the Liaison Committee; opposition days; legislative committees; motions and confidence votes. AO2 — developed analysis: PMQs (public accountability and agenda-setting, but adversarial theatre); select committees (cross-party expertise, elected chairs since the 2010 Wright reforms, influential reports — e.g. the Treasury Committee and the 2022 mini-budget; but government may ignore findings); urgent questions (the Speaker's discretion forces immediate ministerial answers); votes (the ultimate sanction — Callaghan's 1979 confidence loss; May's record 2019 defeats). Synthesis: scrutiny is strongest where publicity and expertise combine (committees) and weakest at the centre (PMQs, whipped majorities). Conclusion: a supported judgement. Edexcel (30 marks) additionally requires: alternative viewpoints (committees vs questions vs votes vs the Lords), a range of contemporary examples, explicit evaluation of 'most effective', and a sustained final judgement that weights the evidence.
practiceQuestions: Explain the term 'Salisbury Convention'. [5 marks]
Analyse the powers of the House of Lords and the factors that limit them. [25 marks]
Evaluate the view that Parliament is effective in holding the executive to account. (30 marks)
Evaluate the view that the House of Lords should be fully elected. (30 marks)
Analyse the main functions of Parliament. [25 marks]

topics.title: The Prime Minister and Cabinet
learningObjectives: Describe the roles and powers of the Prime Minister and of the Cabinet, using key concepts — core executive, primus inter pares, inner cabinet, cabinet committees (AQA 3.1.1.3; Edexcel P2 Topic 3)
Explain the difference between individual and collective ministerial responsibility, supported by named examples such as Crichel Down (1954) and Iain Duncan Smith (2016) (AO1/AO2)
Analyse the factors that shape the relationship between the Prime Minister and the Cabinet: majority size, party unity, cabinet management style and events (AO2)

Deploy case studies of prime ministerial power — one from 1945–1997 (e.g. the poll tax, 1990) and one from 1997 to the present (e.g. the invasion of Iraq, 2003) — as the AQA specification requires (AO1)
Evaluate the 'presidentialism' debate (Foley) using evidence for and against prime ministerial dominance (AO3)
Link prime ministerial power to the other branches — Parliament, the judiciary (Miller II) and devolution — for synoptic credit (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: AQA 3.1.1.3 requires two examples of the PM and Cabinet dictating events: one from 1945–1997 (e.g. poll tax, 1990) and one from 1997–present (e.g. Iraq, 2003).
Collective responsibility has agreed exceptions — the 1975 EEC referendum and the 2016 Brexit referendum allowed Cabinet free votes.
Power depends on circumstance: an 80-seat majority (Johnson 2019) empowers; a hung parliament (May 2017) weakens.
Miller II (2019) struck down prorogation — judicial constraint on the prerogative is now essential evidence in essays.
The 2022 mass ministerial resignations that ended Johnson's premiership show party, not Parliament, is the PM's real check.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the Prime Minister and Cabinet have the power to dictate events and determine policy making (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which the prime minister is able to dominate the cabinet (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 2, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1 (knowledge, ~40%): accurate account of PM powers — patronage, prerogative, media leadership, chairing Cabinet — and the core executive concept; two case studies matching the AQA period requirement (poll tax 1990 pre-1997; Iraq 2003 post-1997). AO2 (analysis, ~30%): factor analysis — majority size (Thatcher 1983/Blair 1997 vs May 2017), party unity (Howe 1990; the 2022 resignations), cabinet management (sofa government vs Truss's exclusion of the Treasury), events (Falklands, COVID, the 2022 markets). AO3 (evaluation, ~30%): a sustained judgement — power is contingent, not presidential: dictation succeeds with landslide majorities and unity (Thatcher, Blair, Johnson 2019) and fails against party (Truss), Parliament (May's 432–202 defeat) and courts (Miller II). Strong answers end by weighing Foley's presidentialism against Hennessy's core executive and concluding on operational variables rather than a flat 'it depends'.
practiceQuestions: Analyse the difference between individual and collective responsibility (AQA, 9 marks)
Explain and analyse three factors that affect the power of the prime minister (Edexcel, 12 marks)
Evaluate the view that the UK prime minister is now effectively a president (Edexcel, 30 marks)
Evaluate the view that prime ministerial power is determined more by circumstances than by personality (AQA, 25 marks)
Explain and analyse three ways in which Parliament can hold the prime minister to account (Edexcel, 12 marks)

topics.title: The Judiciary and Civil Liberties
learningObjectives: Describe the composition of the judiciary and the appointments process — the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, the Supreme Court (2009) and the Judicial Appointments Commission (AQA 3.1.1.4; Edexcel P2 Topic 4)
Distinguish judicial independence from judicial impartiality (neutrality) and evaluate how each is protected or threatened (AO1/AO2)
Explain the role and powers of the Supreme Court: judicial review, ultra vires, statutory interpretation under HRA ss.3 and 4 (AO1/AO2)
Evaluate the impact of Miller I (2017) and Miller II (2019) on the executive, legislature and the policy process (AO2/AO3)
Assess how far the Human Rights Act 1998 protects civil liberties, using cases such as A v SSHD (2004) and PJS v News UK (2016) (AO2/AO3)
Construct balanced judgements on the politicisation of the judiciary and on further reform, linking to the location of sovereignty (AO3)
keyPoints: Miller I (2017, 8–3): triggering Article 50 required an Act of Parliament — the prerogative cannot override statute.
Miller II (2019, 11–0): the five-week prorogation was unlawful, 'void and of no effect' — a direct check on the executive.
A v SSHD (2004, Belmarsh): detention of foreign terror suspects was incompatible with ECHR Arts 5 and 14 — a s.4 declaration that forced the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005.
Declarations of incompatibility do not strike down Acts — parliamentary sovereignty survives Miller I/II.
The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 limited quashing orders and abolished Cart judicial reviews — executive push-back against judicial power.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the UK Supreme Court is now the most powerful branch of government (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which the UK judiciary is independent and impartial (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 2, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate account of composition and appointments (CRA 2005, JAC 2006, Supreme Court 2009), powers (judicial review, ultra vires, HRA s.3/s.4) and key cases — Miller I (2017), Miller II (2019), A v SSHD (2004), UNISON (2017), PJS (2016). AO2: analysis of the Court's impact on the executive and legislature (forcing the EU (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017; voiding prorogation; Belmarsh forcing new terror legislation) balanced against its limits (cannot strike down Acts; Sewel non-justiciable; Parliament ignored Hirst). AO3: sustained judgement — the Court is a genuine but deliberately limited check: 'most powerful branch' overstates because parliamentary sovereignty survives (s.4, Miller I) and the executive pushed back legislatively (DCPA 2022, JRCA 2022); on independence/impartiality versions, conclude that independence is institutionally robust (tenure, JAC, rulings against both parties) while impartiality concerns from elite composition are real but weakening.
practiceQuestions: Analyse the importance of ultra vires and judicial review (AQA, 9 marks)
Explain and analyse three ways in which judicial independence is protected (Edexcel, 12 marks)
Evaluate the impact of the Supreme Court on government, legislature and the policy process (AQA, 25 marks)
Evaluate the extent to which the UK judiciary is both independent and impartial (Edexcel, 30 marks)
Evaluate the view that the Human Rights Act 1998 has done more to protect civil liberties in the UK than any other constitutional reform since 1997 (Edexcel, 30 marks)

topics.title: Democracy and Participation
learningObjectives: Distinguish direct from representative democracy and assess the advantages of each with UK examples (AQA 3.1.2.1; Edexcel P1 Topic 1)
Evaluate claims that the UK suffers a participation crisis, using turnout, party membership and partisan dealignment data (AO2/AO3)
Trace the development of the franchise from the Great Reform Act (1832) to the present, with the roles of the Chartists, Suffragists and Suffragettes (AO1)
Analyse the influence of pressure groups, think tanks, lobbyists and corporations on government and Parliament (AQA 3.1.2.4; Edexcel P1 Topic 1.4)
Evaluate democratic reforms since 1997 — devolution, the HRA, referendums, Lords reform, recall — and remaining deficits (AO2/AO3)
Construct top-band judgements on franchise extension, compulsory voting and the health of UK democracy (AO3)
keyPoints: Turnout collapsed to 59.4% in 2001 but recovered to 67.3% (2019) — the participation crisis is contested, not settled.
2016 EU referendum: 72% turnout, 52–48 — the biggest act of direct democracy in UK history.
Franchise milestones: 1832 → 1867 → 1884 → 1918 → 1928 → 1969 (age 18); Chartists, Suffragists, Suffragettes drove change.
Recall of MPs Act 2015 triggered two by-elections (Onasanya and Davies, both 2019) — first successful recalls in UK history.
Other influences named in both specs: think tanks (Policy Exchange, IPPR), lobbyists (Transparency of Lobbying Act 2014), corporations (CBI) and the media.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the UK is now suffering from a participation crisis (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which democracy in the UK would be improved by further reform (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate data and examples — turnout (84% in 1950, 59.4% in 2001, 72% in 2016), party membership (millions in the 1950s to under 500,000), partisan dealignment, referendums (1975, 2011, 2016, Scottish 2014), e-petitions (2019 revoke petition, 6.1m), franchise acts (1832–1969), reforms since 1997 (devolution, HRA, FOIA, Lords Act 1999, Recall Act 2015). AO2: analysis in both directions — for crisis: turnout, membership, trust post-expenses, safe seats; against: referendum turnout surges, online activism, pressure-group membership. AO3: sustained judgement — participation has migrated from parties and elections to causes and referendums rather than collapsed; 'crisis' requires a threshold the data does not uniformly meet; for reform versions, conclude reform widened participation but left institutional power (Lords, FPTP, executive dominance) largely intact.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three features of direct democracy in the UK (AQA, 9 marks)
Analyse how suffrage has changed since the Great Reform Act of 1832 (AQA, 9 marks)
Evaluate the extent to which the UK suffers from a participation crisis (Edexcel, 30 marks)
Evaluate the view that pressure groups enhance democracy in the UK (AQA, 25 marks)
Evaluate the extent to which the franchise should be extended to 16-year-olds (Edexcel, 30 marks)

topics.title: Political Parties
learningObjectives: Outline the functions performed by political parties — representation, participation, policy formulation, leadership recruitment, mobilisation and government formation — and classify the UK party system (AQA 3.1.2.3; Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Explain how the main parties are organised and funded, and evaluate the case for and against state funding of political parties (AQA 3.1.2.3; Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Trace the ideological and policy development of the Conservative Party from one-nation conservatism through the New Right to modernisation and beyond (Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Trace the ideological and policy development of the Labour Party from democratic socialism through New Labour's Third Way to Corbynism and Starmerism (Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Explain the origins, policies and influence of the Liberal Democrats and of minor parties, including the SNP, Greens, UKIP/Brexit Party and Reform UK (AO1/AO2)
Evaluate the view that the main parties have converged on the centre ground, and assess the effects of convergence and divergence on choice, mandates and the party system (AO2/AO3)
Construct balanced judgements on the emerging UK party system and on the factors that affect party success (AO3)
keyPoints: Functions of parties: representation, participation, policy formulation, leadership recruitment, electoral mobilisation, government formation and opposition.
UK party systems: two-party (1945–70s), Conservative dominance (1979–97), two-and-a-half party (1997–2010), multiparty era since 2010 (coalition, SNP surge, DUP confidence-and-supply, Reform 2024).
Funding: membership, donations, union affiliation fees (Labour), Short money and Cranborne money; PPERA 2000 governs disclosure and spending; scandals fuel the state-funding debate.
Conservative development: Tamworth Manifesto (1834) → one-nation → Thatcherism/New Right → Cameron modernisation → Johnson's levelling up → Truss → 2024 defeat.
Labour development: Clause IV (1918) → Attlee's welfare state → SDP split (1981) → New Labour Third Way → Corbynism → Starmer's fiscal rules.
Convergence narrows voter choice and weakens exclusive mandates; divergence returned over Brexit and in 2024 (tax, immigration, net zero).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the UK is moving towards a multiparty system (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which the policies of the Conservative and Labour parties have converged since 1997 (Edexcel 9PL0, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate account of party functions and system classification (two-party 1945–70s, Conservative dominance 1979–97, multiparty since 2010), funding rules (PPERA 2000, Short money) and party development with named leaders and policies (Thatcher's privatisation, Blair's Clause IV revision, Starmer's fiscal rules). AO2: analysis of convergence — Butskellism, New Labour's acceptance of spending plans and PFI, Cameron's NHS pledge and Big Society, Starmer's fiscal rules — against divergence — Brexit, the 2019 and 2024 manifestos, Labour's employer NI rise versus Reform's tax cuts; analysis of multiparty evidence (2010 coalition, SNP 56 seats, DUP confidence-and-supply, Reform and Green gains) against FPTP's two-party pull (Duverger's law; Labour and Conservative still forming governments). AO3: justified judgement with criteria — voter choice, mandates, representation and accountability — e.g. voting has fragmented but government formation remains two-party, so the UK is best seen as a two-party system with an emerging multiparty electorate; convergence has narrowed economic policy but cultural and constitutional issues now carry the differentiation, sustaining minor-party growth.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three functions performed by political parties in UK politics. [AQA 7152, 9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which party funding creates problems for UK democracy. [Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, 12 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which the Labour Party remains a socialist party. [Edexcel 9PL0, 30 marks]
Evaluate the view that minor parties have little influence on UK politics. [Edexcel 9PL0, 30 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which the Conservative Party remains committed to one-nation conservatism. [AQA 7152, 25 marks]

topics.title: Liberalism: Classical and Modern
learningObjectives: State the six core themes of liberalism (individualism, freedom, rationalism, equality and social justice, the state, liberal democracy) and attach a named thinker to each (AQA 3.3.1; Edexcel 9PL0 core political ideas) (AO1).
Distinguish classical from modern liberalism on the meaning of freedom, the role of the state and the nature of equality, citing Locke, Mill, Rawls and Friedan (AO1/AO2).
Explain why Hobbes is quoted in liberal debates for his state-of-nature and social-contract method despite illiberal conclusions (AO2).
Analyse tensions within liberalism - negative vs positive freedom, atomistic vs developmental individualism, minimal vs enabling state - and judge how fundamental they are (AO2/AO3).
Apply liberal ideas to liberal democracy: consent, constitutionalism, toleration, rule of law (AO2).
Construct balanced essay arguments with substantiated judgements that meet AQA 25-mark extract criteria and Edexcel 30-mark essay criteria (AO3).
keyPoints: Shared ground of all liberals: humans are rational; individuals have equal moral worth; the state must rest on consent, be limited by law and protect rights.
Classical strand (Locke, Mill, Nozick): negative freedom, minimal night-watchman state, laissez-faire economics, formal equality and meritocracy.
Modern strand (Green, Rawls, Friedan): positive freedom, enabling welfare state, managed capitalism, social justice as fairness.
The central tension is the meaning of freedom and the size of the state - crystallised in Nozick vs Rawls over redistribution ('forced labour' vs the difference principle).
Friedan applies liberal individualism to gender: legal equality is empty without tackling cultural conditioning ('the problem that has no name').
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain and analyse three ways in which liberal thinkers have supported the concept of the state. [9 marks] (AQA 7152 Paper 3 style) --- AND --- To what extent do liberals agree about the role of the state? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, core political ideas)
topics.modelAnswer: 9-marker: three points, each claim + thinker + analysis. (1) Locke - the state is created by consent through the social contract to protect natural rights (life, liberty, property); without it, rights are insecure in the state of nature. (2) Mill - the state is justified by the harm principle: it may restrain only other-regarding actions, leaving self-regarding liberty untouched. (3) Rawls - the enabling state is what rational individuals behind the veil of ignorance would consent to: equal basic liberties plus the difference principle. The 30-marker additionally needs: agreements (the state as a necessary evil, limited by law, resting on consent, protecting property); disagreements (minimal vs enabling state; negative vs positive freedom; Nozick's 'forced labour' claim vs Rawls' difference principle); a substantiated judgement (e.g. the strands agree the state must be consent-based and limited but diverge radically on how large it should be - or that moderns extend Locke rather than contradict him); balanced paragraphs with counter-arguments and dated key works.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three ways in which liberal thinkers have supported the idea of freedom. [9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which liberal ideas have influenced liberal democracy. [9 marks]
To what extent do modern liberals differ from classical liberals? [25 marks] (AQA-style essay practice - in the real paper this is extract-based)
To what extent do liberals agree about human nature? [30 marks]
To what extent do liberals support democracy? [30 marks]

topics.title: Conservatism: Traditional and New Right
learningObjectives: State the core themes of conservatism - pragmatism, tradition, human imperfection, organic society, paternalism, property (AQA 3.3.2; Edexcel 9PL0 core political ideas) - with thinker anchors (AO1).
Distinguish traditional/One-Nation conservatism from the New Right, citing Hobbes, Burke, Oakeshott, Rand and Nozick (AO1/AO2).
Explain the two halves of the New Right (neo-liberalism and neo-conservatism) and the internal tension between them (AO2).
Analyse tensions over change, the state, society and the economy, and judge how far conservatism is a coherent ideology (AO2/AO3).
Apply conservatism in practice: Thatcherism's rolling back of the state and the One-Nation post-war consensus (AO2).
Construct balanced essay arguments with substantiated judgements that meet AQA 25-mark and Edexcel 30-mark criteria (AO3).
keyPoints: Shared ground of all conservatives: property, order, tradition broadly defined, human imperfection, and incremental reform ('change to conserve').
Traditional/One-Nation strand (Hobbes, Burke, Oakeshott): paternalism, organic society, pragmatism, acceptance of the post-war welfare settlement.
New Right combines neo-liberal economics (Rand, Nozick) with neo-conservative social policy; its society is atomistic, not organic.
Sharpest tension: organic paternalism vs atomistic self-ownership - welfare as duty vs welfare as 'forced labour'.
The New Right looks ideological, breaching Oakeshott's pragmatism - but its defenders call it pragmatism responding to the 1970s crisis.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain and analyse three ways in which conservative thinkers have viewed human nature. [9 marks] (AQA 7152 Paper 3 style) --- AND --- To what extent do conservatives agree about the role of the state? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, core political ideas)
topics.modelAnswer: 9-marker: three points, each claim + thinker + analysis. (1) Hobbes - humans are driven by fear and appetite, morally and intellectually imperfect; they need an overwhelming sovereign to escape the war of all against all. (2) Oakeshott - humans are intellectually imperfect and cannot design society from first principles; politics must be pragmatic improvisation guided by tradition. (3) Rand - humans are rational and self-interested; imperfection claims are rejected because state welfare saps self-reliance, so self-ownership demands the minimal state. The 30-marker additionally needs: agreements (order, property, tradition, incremental change, human imperfection broadly); disagreements (paternalistic vs minimal state; organic vs atomistic society; welfare as duty vs welfare as 'forced labour'; Keynesian vs monetarist economics); a substantiated judgement (e.g. the New Right is ideological and breaks with Burkean/Oakeshottian pragmatism - or is pragmatism responding to the 1970s crisis); balanced paragraphs with counter-arguments and dated key works.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three ways in which conservative thinkers have supported the idea of tradition. [9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which the ideas of the New Right have influenced conservatism. [9 marks]
To what extent do conservatives agree about human nature? [30 marks]
To what extent is conservatism an ideology rather than a pragmatic disposition? [30 marks]
To what extent have conservatives supported paternalism? [30 marks]

topics.title: Socialism: Revolutionary and Democratic
learningObjectives: State the core themes of socialism - equality, social justice, common ownership, class, workers' control (AQA 3.3.3; Edexcel 9PL0 core political ideas) - with thinker anchors (AO1).
Distinguish revolutionary from democratic socialism, citing Marx, Engels, Luxemburg, Webb and Crosland (AO1/AO2).
Explain the Third Way (Giddens) and assess how far it breaks from earlier socialism (AO2).
Analyse tensions over means, ownership, equality and the role of the state, and judge how far socialism is a coherent ideology (AO2/AO3).
Apply socialism to Labour Party history: Clause IV (1918) and its revision (1995) (AO2).
Construct balanced essay arguments with substantiated judgements that meet AQA 25-mark and Edexcel 30-mark criteria (AO3).
keyPoints: Shared ground of all socialists: equality, community, cooperation, social justice, and a critique of unrestrained capitalism.
Revolutionary strand (Marx, Engels, Luxemburg): class struggle, common ownership, revolution - though Luxemburg insists revolution must be spontaneous and democratic.
Democratic strand (Webb, Crosland): gradualism via the ballot box, nationalisation then welfare, mixed economy.
Third Way (Giddens): equality of opportunity, social investment, communitarianism - it accepts the market and globalisation.
Sharpest tensions: means (revolution vs reform) and ends (common ownership vs regulated market); Clause IV 1918 vs 1995 dramatises both.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain and analyse three ways in which socialist thinkers have viewed equality. [9 marks] (AQA 7152 Paper 3 style) --- AND --- To what extent do socialists agree about the economy? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, core political ideas)
topics.modelAnswer: 9-marker: three points, each claim + thinker + analysis. (1) Marx - equality of outcome in communism: 'to each according to his needs'; class and exploitation abolished through common ownership. (2) Crosland - equality of opportunity and fair distribution through the welfare state and comprehensive education, not common ownership; social justice is the goal. (3) Giddens - equality of opportunity via social investment (education, skills); relative poverty matters but incentives are preserved. The 30-marker additionally needs: agreements (equality as the core value, social justice, community and cooperation, criticism of unrestrained capitalism); disagreements (common ownership vs mixed economy vs regulated market; revolution vs ballot box; outcome vs opportunity); a substantiated judgement (e.g. socialists agree on ends but divide on route and destination - or that the Third Way's acceptance of the market abandons the core); balanced paragraphs with counter-arguments and dated key works.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three ways in which socialist thinkers have supported common ownership. [9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which socialist thinkers have viewed class. [9 marks]
To what extent do socialists agree about the means of achieving socialism? [30 marks]
To what extent have socialists supported equality of outcome over equality of opportunity? [30 marks]
To what extent did the Third Way abandon socialism? [30 marks]

topics.title: US Politics: Comparative Politics
learningObjectives: Outline the three comparative theories - rational choice, cultural and structural - and apply each to a US/UK difference or similarity (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 3, comparative theories) (AO1/AO2).
Compare the US codified constitution and federalism with the UK's uncodified, unitary-devolved arrangement (AO1/AO2).
Compare Congress with Parliament and the presidency with the premiership, including divided government, checks and gridlock (AO2).
Compare the US Supreme Court's powers and appointment process with the UK Supreme Court, and civil rights protection in both (AO2).
Compare US and UK elections, parties and participation, including the Electoral College, primaries and campaign finance (AO2).
Write comparative essays that synthesise US and UK content and use comparative theories to reach substantiated judgements (AO3).
keyPoints: Comparative essays demand synthesis: two-way comparison plus explicit use of rational choice, cultural or structural theory - not parallel description of each system.
Constitutions: US codified and entrenched (27 amendments since 1787) vs UK uncodified and flexible; separation of powers vs parliamentary fusion.
Executive: president checks Congress (veto, appointments) but faces gridlock under divided government; PM fuses executive and legislature and usually dominates it.
Courts: US Supreme Court strikes down legislation (Marbury 1803) with politicised appointments; UK Supreme Court (2009) only declares incompatibility under HRA s.4.
Elections: fixed terms, Electoral College swing-state focus and popular-vote splits (2000, 2016) vs UK flexible dates, FPTP and referendums.
topics.exampleQuestion: To what extent is the US presidency more powerful than the UK premiership? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 3, Section B) --- AND --- Using the comparative theories, to what extent are the US and UK constitutions similar? [30 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Presidency question: AO1 - accurate comparative knowledge (formal powers: veto, appointments, Commander-in-Chief vs royal assent, patronage, collective responsibility; fixed terms; divided government). AO2 - analysis of strengths and limits: the president checks Congress but faces gridlock under divided government and reversals of executive orders; the PM fuses executive and legislature and usually dominates, but is checked by party rebellion and lost majorities. AO3 - judgement with criteria: domestically the PM is usually more powerful (fusion, majority, control of the legislative timetable); in foreign affairs the president is stronger (Commander-in-Chief, executive agreements); structural theory explains the contrast (separation vs fusion). Constitutional question: AO1 - codified vs uncodified, entrenchment, separation of powers vs fusion, federal vs unitary-devolved, entrenched Bill of Rights vs HRA. AO2 - similarities (both limit government, protect rights, establish representative democracy) and differences (rigidity vs flexibility; judicial supremacy vs parliamentary sovereignty). AO3 - judgement: more different than similar, or vice versa, with criteria and a named theory applied throughout.
practiceQuestions: To what extent are the US and UK constitutions similar? [30 marks]
To what extent is Congress more powerful than Parliament? [30 marks]
To what extent are the US Supreme Court and UK Supreme Court similar? [30 marks]
To what extent does the Electoral College undermine US democracy? [30 marks]
To what extent are rational choice theory and cultural theory useful for comparing US and UK politics? [30 marks]

topics.title: The English Legal System
learningObjectives: Describe the hierarchy of the civil courts (County Court, High Court, Court of Appeal, Supreme Court) and apply the track system (small claims, fast, intermediate, multi) to a claim scenario (AQA 3.1.1; OCR H418 Component 1; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)
Set out the criminal court structure, including the summary/either-way/indictable classification and the magistrates' plea-before-venue and mode-of-trial procedures
Trace appeal routes in both systems, including case stated, second appeals (Access to Justice Act 1999 s.55), leapfrog appeals (Administration of Justice Act 1969) and appeals to the Supreme Court
Distinguish civil from criminal law using purpose, parties, terminology, remedies and the standards of proof (Woolmington v DPP; Miller v Minister of Pensions)
Explain the role, appointment and independence of the judiciary, citing the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, Pinochet (No 2) and Miller (No 2)
Apply the rules on jury qualification, selection, disqualification and majority verdicts (Juries Act 1974 s.17; Bushel's Case; R v Ponting), and evaluate jury equity
Compare court and non-court dispute resolution (negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, tribunals, ombudsmen) and assess access to justice after LASPO 2012
keyPoints: Civil hierarchy: County Court → High Court (KBD, Chancery, Family) → Court of Appeal (Civil Division) → Supreme Court.
Criminal hierarchy: Magistrates' Court → Crown Court → Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) → Supreme Court.
Criminal standard: beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington v DPP). Civil standard: balance of probabilities (Miller v Minister of Pensions).
Magistrates deal with roughly 95% of criminal cases; juries of 12 try indictable offences in the Crown Court.
Majority verdicts: 10:1, or 9:1 if the panel has been reduced, after at least 2 hours (Juries Act 1974 s.17).
CCRC (Criminal Appeal Act 1995) refers suspected miscarriages of justice back to the Court of Appeal.
LASPO 2012 cut civil legal aid; funding now relies heavily on CFAs, ombudsmen and free advice services.
topics.exampleQuestion: Priya is suing her former landlord in the County Court for £35,000 in damages for disrepair and personal injury. Separately, her neighbour Theo is charged with unlawful wounding (either-way) after an argument in the street. (a) Explain which track Priya's claim is likely to be allocated and how it could be appealed. (b) Explain how Theo's case will proceed through the criminal courts, including appeal routes, and how the standard of proof differs between his case and Priya's. [OCR H418 Component 1 style scenario; AQA Paper 1 style — 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 — state the law: (a) civil hierarchy — County Court, High Court divisions, Court of Appeal (Civil Division), Supreme Court; track system under CPR 1998: small claims (under £10,000; £1,000 for PI), fast track (£10,000–£25,000), intermediate track (£25,000–£100,000, fixed recoverable costs from 2023), multi-track (complex/high value); appeal routes: next level of judge/High Court, second appeal test (Access to Justice Act 1999 s.55 — important point of principle/practice or compelling reason), leapfrog (Administration of Justice Act 1969). (b) criminal classification — summary, either-way, indictable only; plea before venue and mode of trial; magistrates' powers (6 months per offence; 12 months total); Crown Court for trial before judge and jury; appeals — defendant: s.108 MCA 1980 to Crown Court, case stated s.111 to High Court, Crown Court to CoA Crim Div if unsafe (Criminal Appeal Act 1968); prosecution: no appeal against acquittal, A-G's reference on point of law (CJA 1972 s.36), unduly lenient sentences (CJA 1988 s.36); CCRC (Criminal Appeal Act 1995); standards of proof — beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington v DPP) for the prosecution, balance of probabilities (Miller v Minister of Pensions) for Priya as claimant. AO2 — apply: Priya's claim is £35,000 including personal injury above £1,000, so small claims is excluded; £35,000 falls in the intermediate track (fixed recoverable costs), appealed to a High Court judge then CoA (Civil Division) only with permission under the s.55 second-appeal test; leapfrog only if a certified point of law arises with consent. Theo's wounding is either-way: he pleads before venue; if he pleads not guilty, magistrates decide mode of trial — likely acceptable and suitable, but given injury severity may send to Crown Court; appeal by defendant via s.108 to Crown Court or case stated to High Court (s.111), or from Crown Court to CoA Crim Div if conviction unsafe. The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington); Priya must prove her claim only on the balance of probabilities (Miller) — Theo's burden is heavier because liberty is at stake. AO3 — evaluate: tracks prioritise proportionality (Woolf aims — cost, speed, fairness); fixed recoverable costs control expense but may squeeze representation; the criminal/civil proof gap prevents inconsistent punishment but can produce apparently conflicting verdicts (O J Simpson); CCRC and relaxed double jeopardy (CJA 2003; R v Dunlop; R v Dobson) balance finality with correcting miscarriages of justice.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish civil law from criminal law. Refer to purpose, parties, standard of proof and outcomes. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Describe the appeal routes from a magistrates' court and from the Crown Court. [OCR H418 Component 1, 10 marks]
Explain how juries are qualified, selected and controlled, and evaluate the idea of jury equity. [WJEC/Eduqas Component 1, 15 marks]

Theo is dismissed and claims unfair dismissal. His employer wants arbitration; Theo wants to go to an employment tribunal. Explain arbitration and tribunals, then evaluate which suits Theo better. [OCR H418 Component 1, 20 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which LASPO 2012 and cuts to civil legal aid have undermined access to justice. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

topics.title: Parliamentary Law Making and Delegated Legislation
learningObjectives: Trace the full legislative process — Green and White Papers, bill types (public, private, hybrid, private members'), all stages in both Houses, ping-pong and Royal Assent — citing the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 (AQA 3.1.2; OCR H418 Component 3, Section A; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)
Explain the influences on parliamentary law making, including pressure groups (Snowdrop campaign), the media, public opinion and the Law Commission under the Law Commissions Act 1965
Distinguish the three types of delegated legislation — statutory instruments, byelaws and Orders in Council — with examples, and explain why Parliament delegates (AQA 3.1.3)
Apply parliamentary controls: enabling act limits, affirmative and negative resolutions (Statutory Instruments Act 1946), the Joint Select Committee on Statutory Instruments and Henry VIII clauses
