topics.title: Epistemology: Perception, Knowledge and Gettier
learningObjectives: Define knowledge using the tripartite (justified true belief) view and construct Gettier-style counter-examples against it (Spec 3.1.1).
Explain and evaluate direct realism, indirect realism and Berkeleian idealism, including illusion, hallucination and veil-of-perception issues (Spec 3.1.2).
Explain Plato's innate knowledge thesis and Descartes' intuition and deduction thesis, with Locke's and Hume's critiques (Spec 3.1.3).
Distinguish a priori from a posteriori knowledge and apply Hume's fork to a priori claims about the world.
Analyse and evaluate philosophical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent').
Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays.
keyPoints: Gettier cases show JTB is not sufficient for knowledge: true belief + justification + epistemic luck is not knowledge.
Direct realism: perception is immediate awareness of physical objects; attacked by perceptual variation, illusion, hallucination and time-lag.
Indirect realism (Locke): we perceive the world via sense-data; attacked by the veil of perception, answered by Russell's inference to the best explanation.
Idealism (Berkeley): only minds and ideas exist; the master argument plus God's perception; attacked on the act/object conflation and pre-mind worlds.
Rationalism (Plato, Descartes) grounds knowledge in reason; empiricism (Locke, Hume) in experience; Hume's fork restricts a priori knowledge to relations of ideas.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Indirect realism means we can never know anything about the external world.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: define indirect realism (we perceive mind-independent objects indirectly via sense-data; Locke; primary/secondary qualities); explain the veil-of-perception and sceptical issues — if only sense-data are perceived, their causal link to external objects is unverifiable and the world's existence does not follow. AO2 required: argue with intent, e.g. AGAINST the claim — (1) inference to the best explanation (Russell): mind-independent objects are the best explanation of the involuntary, coherent and unpredictable pattern of sense-data, so indirect realism licenses a posteriori knowledge of the world; (2) cross-sensory coherence: what I see I can touch, which dream/demon hypotheses explain less well. Consider the strongest objection FOR the claim: best explanation is only inductive — a demon or brain-in-a-vat hypothesis explains the same data, so the inference underdetermines and yields at most probability, not knowledge; respond: demanding deductive certainty sets the bar higher than empirical science meets anywhere, and reliability, not certainty, is the right standard for knowledge. Weigh up and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim fails: indirect realism, via best explanation, secures fallible but genuine knowledge of the external world).
practiceQuestions: Explain the tripartite view of knowledge. (5 marks)
Explain Gettier-style problems for the tripartite view of knowledge and one response. (12 marks)
Explain Berkeley's 'master argument' for idealism. (5 marks)
Explain Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities. (5 marks)
'Berkeley's idealism is more convincing than indirect realism.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Scepticism and Descartes' Meditations
learningObjectives: Distinguish normal incredulity from philosophical scepticism and set out Descartes' method of doubt (Spec 3.1.4).
Explain the dreaming and evil demon arguments with their premises and conclusions.
Explain the cogito and Descartes' clear and distinct ideas thesis, including the charge of the Cartesian circle.
Explain the problem of other minds with the argument from analogy and the 'best hypothesis' response (Spec 3.1.4).
Evaluate sceptical arguments and their responses to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2).
Answer 3/5/12-mark questions with pure AO1 explanation, using correct command-word technique.
keyPoints: Descartes' method of doubt is a search for certainty, not an endorsement of scepticism — sceptical arguments are his tools.
The evil demon is the strongest sceptical scenario because it attacks reason (mathematics) as well as the senses.
The cogito survives all doubt: 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever it is thought.
The Cartesian circle: clear and distinct ideas prove God; God guarantees clear and distinct ideas — Descartes' reply turns on present attention vs memory.
The problem of other minds is answered by the argument from analogy and the 'best hypothesis' response — both inductive, never deductive.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Descartes' sceptical arguments show we cannot know anything beyond our own minds.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: set out the method of doubt, the dreaming argument (no infallible marks; dreams present non-existent things; so the senses cannot give knowledge of the external world), the evil demon (supreme deceiver attacks mathematics as well as the senses), the cogito ('I am, I exist' — necessarily true whenever thought), the clear and distinct ideas truth rule, and the Cartesian circle charge. AO2 — argue with intent, e.g. AGAINST the claim: (1) the cogito defeats the demon: doubting presupposes thinking, so 'I am, I exist' is indubitable — knowledge beyond doubt survives, though only about my own mind at the moment of thought; (2) the dreaming argument localises: it removes knowledge of particular external objects at particular times, not all knowledge. Consider the strongest objection FOR the claim: the evil demon attacks even a priori beliefs, and the Cartesian circle means God never certifies clear and distinct ideas — so nothing beyond the cogito is secure. Respond: Descartes' remembered-vs-present distinction blocks the circle (self-evidence needs no guarantee while attending; God secures memory), and if that fails, the reliabilist route still leaves fallible knowledge of the world. Weigh up and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim overstates: global scepticism is not established, but knowledge beyond one's own mind does require rejecting Descartes' standard of certainty).
practiceQuestions: Explain the difference between ordinary incredulity and philosophical scepticism. (5 marks)
Explain Descartes' dreaming argument and one response. (12 marks)
Explain the problem of other minds and the argument from analogy. (12 marks)
Explain Descartes' cogito. (5 marks)
'The argument from analogy successfully answers the problem of other minds.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Moral Philosophy: Utilitarianism, Kant and Aristotelian Virtue Ethics
learningObjectives: Explain and evaluate Bentham's act utilitarianism (hedonism, felicific calculus) and Mill's qualitative, rule-based refinement (Spec 3.2.1).
Explain and evaluate Kantian deontology: the good will, duty, the categorical imperative's formulations and clashing-duty issues (Spec 3.2.1).
Explain and evaluate Aristotelian virtue ethics: eudaimonia, the function argument, the doctrine of the mean and phronesis (Spec 3.2.1).
Apply utilitarianism, Kantian deontology and virtue ethics to stealing, eating animals, simulated killing and telling lies (Spec 3.2.2).
Compare the three theories' decision procedures, strengths and weaknesses to form reasoned judgements (AO2).
Write 25-mark essays 'arguing with intent' with balanced argument sandwiches and consistent conclusions.
keyPoints: Bentham: quantitative hedonism + felicific calculus; Mill: qualitative pleasures + rule utilitarianism + competent-judges 'proof'.
Kant: act from duty via the categorical imperative — universal law, humanity as an end, kingdom of ends; consequences are irrelevant to rightness.
Aristotle: eudaimonia via the function argument; virtues are means between vices, hit by practical wisdom and habituation.
Classic critiques: tyranny of the majority and integrity (utilitarianism); clashing duties and rigidity (Kant); circularity and guidance (Aristotle).
Applied ethics on spec: stealing, eating animals, simulated killing, telling lies — each theory delivers a different verdict.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Utilitarianism is a better account of morality than Kantian ethics.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: set out Bentham's act utilitarianism (hedonism, felicific calculus) and Mill's refinement (higher/lower pleasures, rule utilitarianism); set out Kantian ethics (good will, duty vs inclination, universal law and humanity formulations, with the false-promise example). AO2 — argue with intent, e.g. FOR utilitarianism: (1) moral reach: sentience, not rational nature, grounds moral status (Bentham), so utilitarianism captures duties to animals and future people that Kant cannot; (2) flexibility: consequences matter — refusing to lie to the murderer at the door (Kant/Constant) is intuitively unacceptable. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST: aggregation permits injustice — punishing the innocent to stop a riot (tyranny of the majority) and Jim and the Indians (Williams' integrity) show utilitarianism alienates agents from morality; respond: rule utilitarianism forbids such acts by general-utility rules. Counter-response: extreme scenarios (overruling a rule would save everyone) reveal rule utilitarianism collapsing back into act utilitarianism. Weigh up: utilitarianism's reach and flexibility vs Kant's absolute protection of persons; conclude consistently (either direction is defensible if argued with intent — e.g. Kantian ethics better respects dignity, but utilitarianism better handles real cases).
practiceQuestions: Explain Bentham's felicific calculus. (5 marks)
Explain Kant's universal law formulation of the categorical imperative and how it applies to false promising. (12 marks)
Explain Aristotle's function argument. (5 marks)
Explain Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures. (5 marks)
'Kantian ethics cannot be applied in practice.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Metaethics: Cognitivism, Realism and Moral Language
learningObjectives: Distinguish the two metaethical axes — cognitivism vs non-cognitivism and realism vs anti-realism — and locate each theory on both axes (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain the possible origins of moral principles in reason, in emotion/attitudes or in society (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain moral naturalism, including naturalist forms of utilitarianism (Bentham) and of virtue ethics, and evaluate it using Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain moral non-naturalism — Moore's intuitionism and Ross's prima facie duties — and evaluate the challenges from Hume's fork, the is-ought gap and the motivation argument (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain Mackie's error theory — the arguments from relativity and from queerness — and assess the nihilism charge (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain and evaluate emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson) and prescriptivism (Hare), including whether anti-realism can account for moral reasoning, disagreement and moral progress (Spec 3.2.3).
Analyse and evaluate metaethical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent').
keyPoints: Two independent axes: cognitivism (moral judgements truth-apt) vs non-cognitivism (not truth-apt); realism (mind-independent moral facts) vs anti-realism (none). Every theory sits on both.
Moral principles may originate in reason (Moore, Ross), emotion/attitudes (Ayer) or society (Mackie: 'inventing' right and wrong).
Naturalism: good = natural property — Bentham: pleasure; naturalist virtue ethics: flourishing. Attacked by Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy.

Non-naturalism (Moore, Ross): good is simple, non-natural, known by intuition; Ross adds plural, self-evident prima facie duties. Attacked by Hume's fork, the is-ought gap, the motivation argument and Mackie's queerness.

Error theory (Mackie): judgements aim at objective truth but all fail — arguments from relativity and queerness; nihilism charge. Emotivism (boo/hurrah, persuasion) and prescriptivism (universalisable prescriptions) deny truth-aptness; attacked via embedded contexts, disagreement, the fanatic and moral progress.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Moral judgements do not state facts but express emotions.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: define the axes — cognitivism (moral judgements state propositions and are truth-apt; naturalism: Bentham's good = pleasure; non-naturalism: Moore's simple non-natural property known by intuition) vs non-cognitivism (moral judgements express non-cognitive states, not truth-apt); explain emotivism — Ayer's verification principle (moral judgements neither analytic nor empirically verifiable, so they state nothing) and the boo/hurrah analysis, plus Stevenson's emotive meaning and persuasive function. AO2 required — argue with intent, e.g. FOR the claim: (1) Hume's motivation argument — beliefs alone are inert but moral judgements reliably motivate, so they are not pure beliefs but expressions of attitude; (2) Mackie's argument from relativity — persistent cross-cultural disagreement is best explained by different ways of life, not by misperception of mind-independent facts; (3) the verificationist point that no observation confirms 'stealing is wrong'. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST: the embedded-context (Frege–Geach) problem — 'if stealing is wrong, getting your little brother to steal is wrong' is valid, yet the unasserted antecedent expresses no emotion, so moral claims must retain truth-apt meaning; and moral disagreement is genuine contradiction supported by reasons on both sides, not a clash of cheers — Stevenson's 'persuasion' analysis re-describes rather than explains it. Respond: sophisticated non-cognitivism (Hare) treats moral judgements as universalisable prescriptions, allowing reasoning and disagreement within attitudes. Counter-response: prescriptions are not truth-apt either, and the fanatic who universalises consistently shows non-cognitivism cannot capture moral commitment as a stance towards facts. Weigh up and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim overstates: motivation and relativity support expressivism, but the logic of embedded contexts and the reason-giving character of moral disagreement show moral judgements are more than emotional expression — if cognitivism falls, error theory preserves the fact-stating purport better than emotivism).
practiceQuestions: Explain Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy. (5 marks)
Explain Hume's motivation argument and one cognitivist response. (12 marks)
Explain Mackie's argument from queerness. (5 marks)
Explain Hare's claim that moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions. (5 marks)
'Emotivism cannot account for how we use moral language.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Metaphysics of God: Divine Attributes, Arguments and Religious Language
learningObjectives: Explain and evaluate the definitions of God as omnipotent, eternal and omniscient, including the paradox of the stone, Descartes vs Aquinas/Kenny, and Boethius vs Swinburne on eternality (Spec 3.3.1).
Explain and evaluate the ontological argument — Anselm (Proslogion 2 and 3), Descartes and Malcolm — with Gaunilo's perfect-island reply and Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' (Spec 3.3.2).
Explain and evaluate the teleological argument — Paley's watch, Swinburne's regularity — with Hume's critiques and Darwin's theory of evolution (Spec 3.3.2).
Explain and evaluate the cosmological argument — Aquinas' Three Ways, the Kalam argument, Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason — with Hume's and Russell's critiques (Spec 3.3.2).
Explain and evaluate the logical problem of evil (Mackie's inconsistent triad, Plantinga's free will defence) and the evidential problem (Rowe's fawn, Hick's vale of soul-making) (Spec 3.3.3).

Explain and evaluate religious experience (James, Swinburne's credulity and testimony, Flew's verification challenge) and religious language (via negativa, Aquinas' analogy, Ayer, Hare, Hick) (Specs 3.3.4–3.3.5).
Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; 'arguing with intent' and balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays.
keyPoints: Omnipotence (Aquinas/Kenny): every power it is logically possible to have — the stone task is self-contradictory, not a genuine limit; Descartes: God can do the logically impossible, having created the eternal truths.
Boethius: God is timeless — 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life'; foreknowledge becomes timeless seeing, imposing only conditional necessity on free acts.
Ontological (Anselm Proslogion 2/3, Descartes, Malcolm) vs Kant: existence is not a real predicate (100 thalers) — the crucial debate is whether necessary existence escapes Kant.

Cosmological: Aquinas' Three Ways (per se regress), Kalam (no actual infinities), Leibniz (sufficient reason); Hume (fallacy of composition) and Russell ('the universe is just there, and that's all').

Evil: Mackie's triad answered by Plantinga (free will defence + transworld depravity); Rowe's fawn answered by theodicy (Hick) or sceptical theism. Flew's falsification challenge answered by Hare's bliks and Hick's eschatological verification.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Kant is right: existence is not a predicate, and so the ontological argument fails.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: set out Anselm's Proslogion 2 (God = 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; exists in the understanding; greater to exist in reality; contradiction if God existed in the mind alone) and Proslogion 3 (necessary existence), Descartes' 'existence is a perfection' (triangle analogy) and Malcolm's version; explain Kant's critique — existence is not a real predicate ('is' adds no property; 100 real thalers and 100 imagined thalers share one concept). AO2 required: argue with intent, e.g. FOR the claim — (1) if 'is' adds nothing, defining God as existing, or counting existence among the perfections, begs the question: the argument analyses a concept and then asserts the concept is instantiated; (2) Malcolm's 'necessary existence' does not escape: treating a logical status as an attribute repeats exactly the error Kant identifies, so the argument still fails a priori. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST the claim: Kant targets ordinary, contingent existence; necessary existence — existence that cannot be lacked without incoherence — may be a genuine predicate, in which case Proslogion 3 survives, and Anselm's reply to Gaunilo (the argument's form applies to God alone) blocks the 'proves too much' objection; respond: even if necessary existence is a predicate, the move from coherence to instantiation needs defence — conceivability of a necessary being may not entail its instantiation. Weigh up (the crucial debate is Kant vs Malcolm on whether necessary existence is a predicate) and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim fails: Kant refutes arguments from contingent existence, but a modalised ontological argument treating necessary existence as a predicate remains live).
practiceQuestions: Explain the paradox of the stone and one response to it. (5 marks)
Explain Boethius' solution to the problem of God's foreknowledge and human free will. (12 marks)
Explain Aquinas' Third Way. (5 marks)
Explain Mackie's inconsistent triad and Plantinga's free will defence. (12 marks)
'Religious experience is no basis for belief in God because claims about God are unfalsifiable.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Metaphysics of Mind: Dualism, Physicalism and Functionalism
learningObjectives: Explain the mind–body problem and define mental properties via qualia and intentionality (Spec 3.4.1).
Explain and evaluate Descartes' conceivability and divisibility arguments for substance dualism, and Elisabeth of Bohemia's interaction objection with the causal closure argument (Spec 3.4.2).
Explain and evaluate property dualism via Chalmers' zombie argument, including conceivability-vs-possibility and masking critiques (Spec 3.4.2).
Explain and evaluate logical behaviourism (Hempel, Ryle's category mistake) and its circularity, pretence and qualia critiques (Spec 3.4.3).
Explain and evaluate type identity theory (Place, Smart), the multiple realizability objection, and eliminative materialism (Churchlands) with the self-refutation critique (Spec 3.4.3).
Explain and evaluate functionalism (Putnam) via inverted qualia, philosophical zombies and absent qualia (Spec 3.4.4).
Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; argue with intent on 25-mark essays.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Philosophical zombies are conceivable, so physicalism is false.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: define physicalism (all facts, including mental facts, are fixed by physical facts); define philosophical zombies (physically and behaviourally identical to us, no qualia); set out Chalmers' argument: zombies are conceivable; what is conceivable is metaphysically possible; if zombies are possible, physical facts do not determine conscious facts; so physicalism is false. AO2 required: argue with intent, e.g. FOR the claim — (1) qualia are knowable only from the first person (Nagel), so no physical description fixes the feel of experience; (2) zombie scenarios are coherently describable: a world physically identical yet qualitatively empty involves no contradiction. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST: conceivability is not a guide to possibility — Kripke's necessary a posteriori identities (water = H₂O: conceivable without H₂O, yet impossible), and Dennett's charge that zombies are incoherent: a behaviourally identical being making all our consciousness reports would thereby have whatever makes consciousness; respond: Chalmers distinguishes ideal (primary) conceivability from mere imagery and argues ideal conceivability entails possibility; counter-response: that entailment is exactly what physicalists deny — 'zombies are possible' is just physicalism's negation restated, so the argument risks begging the question. Weigh up (e.g. the argument survives as a challenge to reductive physicalism, but functionalist/non-reductive physicalism can resist it) and conclude consistently.
practiceQuestions: Explain the difference between mental and physical properties. (5 marks)
Explain Descartes' divisibility argument for substance dualism. (5 marks)
Explain Elisabeth of Bohemia's objection to substance dualism and Descartes' response. (12 marks)
Explain the multiple realizability objection to type identity theory. (12 marks)
